Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore the connection between these characteristics and the speaker's individual traits, specifically their personality and background. We've conducted an emotional characterization study, gathering ratings of speaker personalities (e.g. warm, competitive) and life experiences (e.g. military service, university education) in addition to their audio recordings. We've analyzed the relationships between these characteristics and the speakers' vocal traits. We've also manipulated the existing synthetic speech models to incorporate the identified acoustic features of warm and competent speakers. Initially, warm females were targeted for modification, as their previous perception as cold was a common issue. We've evaluated the success of our modifications in altering the perceived speaker characteristics. The results show a strong correlation between the modified speech's acoustic properties and the speakers' perceived warmth. In a listening test, our modified speech has been perceived as significantly warmer and the listeners' confidence in the speaker's individuality has increased.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses are produced through one-loop interactions, resulting in a bosonic dark matter candidate within the range of approximately 0.01-50 GeV. Stabilization of dark matter occurs due to a combination of nonzero modular weight and residual Z2 symmetry derived from the U(1)_(B-L) symmetry. Indirect naturalness of dark matter mass arises from radiative mass generation in neutral fermions that interact with dark matter. For a scenario where all elements are zero except for one non-zero texture entry of the neutrino mass matrix at the seesaw scale, numerical analysis reveals that the numerical values of this entry and the higgsino dark matter mass correlate directly. As a result, numerical values of the former, as calculated from the latter's variation, demonstrate the model's capability to account for the Earth's dark matter density observational data across a wide range of scales up to approximately 50 GeV.

Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. A particular feature of triaxial nuclei, accounted for by introducing an inversion symmetry based on the rotational symmetry of their collective motion, is considered essential. Focusing on minimal length correction in algebraic models enables the derivation of collective variables for nuclei with any degree of symmetry, as demonstrated in a study of the ${}^{134}$Ba triaxial nucleus. For the first time, minimal length correction in this context has been implemented, with calculated eigenenergies showing good agreement compared to experimental data. In addition, the associated wave functions for both minimal length correction and linear minimalization techniques were analyzed to uncover the hidden structure of nuclear states. A displacement of minimal length to a point in space, characterized by its expectation value, is observed: this point may exist in both the intrinsic and laboratory frames; its stability against collective motion is ensured; the frame rotation that arises from this motion does not affect the point's location. A theoretical and analytical method for the minimal length concept has been developed, with findings validated through the analysis of a ${}^{134}$Ba nucleus wave disintegration. In a broader sense, the minimal length concept is consistent with the Weizsacker Institute model and its inherent collective parameters. This approach is not limited to isotopic nuclei but can be applied to heavy elements as well.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78, 130x130, and a few others. However, whether all sizes are possible remains an open question.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study presents a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. The proposed method's effectiveness on three diverse hyperspectral image datasets demonstrates its ability to accurately detect changes, even with minimal computational requirements.

A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling the entropic rule of mixtures maintains consistency across a broad selection of pure substances (over 40 different substances) and various models (including pairwise potentials), as well as solutions with like and unlike components. The phenomenon suggests that the structure of molecular fluids exhibits commonalistic properties, which underpins a universal, entropy-based viscosity prediction model that performs well across a wide range of conditions (up to 8 times the normal boiling point, densities spanning two orders of magnitude, and various molecular models).

The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion and contraction has been explored by researchers for a long time. This specific model, known as the Lambda Cold Dark Matter periodic cosmology, suggests that dark energy acts as a negative pressure that drives the collapse once the scale factor exceeds a particular threshold. In the proposed LCDM periodic model, two separate pieces of evidence, the difference in magnitudes of type Ia supernovae and the cosmic microwave background anisotropy data, as well as large scale structure data, indicate that the scale factor peak occurs approximately between 2.82 and 2.97 and approximately at 0.553 and 0.635 cosmic time scale. Additionally, the LCDM periodic model predicts that the current rate of supernova brightness increase for type Ia events should be roughly one to two and a half times the predicted increase based on a model where the scale factor increases indefinitely. In the proposed LCDM periodic model, the predicted and observed values for the Hubble constant, supernovae redshift, and cosmic microwave background anisotropy scale factor do not match, but the discrepancies for these values are relatively small. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea asserts that the underlying space of the hidden variables giving rise to quantum correlations is very small, resulting in the strong correlations seen at low entanglement levels returning to classical expectations in high entanglement levels. In this research, a hidden-variable model is created to analytically examine the Invariant-set theory, with the model's constraints mirroring those of the original theory. It has been discovered that this model cannot explain highly entangled phenomena without exceeding certain boundary limits. Moreover, this model's capacity for explaining certain quantum phenomena like the Bell nonsum rule is limited and requires careful interpretation.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting (KWS) on embedded devices, alongside existing solutions. Our focus is on NN architectures suitable for in-context learning on low-powered IoT devices, using limited training data. We evaluate four lightweight KWS models on an entry-level microcontroller, comparing their training efficiency, accuracy, and memory requirements. Notably, one of the proposed models achieves an impressive 97.4% test classification accuracy for a sparse vocabulary of 20 words, trained on just 29 words, and can be trained and executed in under 1 second on an embedded device. The generated models are made available through our online code repository.

In the case where lattice spacing vanishes, the analysis focuses on the dimer model on isoradial graphs in the presence of $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ gauge fields with zero curl except at specified punctures. The cluster expansion of the partition function for the twisted dimer model is matched with the analogous cluster expansion of the 2D Dirac partition function in this gauge field scenario, also referred to as the tau function. This derivation validates and broadens earlier findings by Dubedat, particularly in regards to the observables at the lattice scale, yet notes a discrepancy in the coefficient for the leading term, coinciding with results from the polyon algebra by Kozlov and the skein relations of the six-vertex model.

Working with categorical data in high-dimensional learning environments necessitates specialized approaches for efficient results. Recent applications have employed the group Lasso method to achieve sparse and regulized estimation, commonly utilizing encoding techniques such as one-hot and orthogonal to represent categorical variables. However, the former introduces redundancy and can lead to inconsistent estimates, while the latter's computational limitations are restrictive due to its inability to exploit sparsity in the orthogonal matrix. Our paper develops a novel method to take advantage of sparsity in both encoding methods, and is further enhanced with an optimized solution technique that leverages accelerated gradient descent and an efficient thresholding function. Our approach's performance is quantified through theoretical guarantees, and extensive experiments confirm its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex and demanding, necessitating the execution of multiple tasks with varying priority levels and safety critical requirements in the same single processing unit. This trend has led to the adoption of virtualization technology in embedded systems, utilizing hypervisors to enable safe and segregated execution of tasks and facilitate efficient system management. This research aims to investigate the feasibility of employing hardware virtualization technologies in embedded systems, specifically by developing a hypervisor, dubbed T-Visor, for safety critical real-time systems. To evaluate the performance of T-Visor, a case study was conducted using the Unix-like VxWorks real-time operating system on x86 architecture. The experimental results indicate that, compared to the native execution of Vxvisor on bare hardware, the overhead of execution on hardware virtualization technologies such as Intel VT-d and Virtualization results in a 3.1% to 5.0% delay in task scheduling. This empirical analysis confirms the effectiveness of T-Visor as a hypervisor for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems with hardware virtualization support.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly. Taking advantage of this common practice, our approach formulates a novel, efficient, and intuitive alignment procedure that exploits the known camera orientation. The method calculates azimuthal alignment through correlation of major scene features, while accounting for varying altitudes through the use of radial distortion in a 2D steady-state Kalman filter. The proposed technique demonstrates superior performance by leveraging the intersection of azimuth and radial distortions to accurately determine the focal length and tilt of each image capture. Experimental results indicate that our method exhibits high accuracy, with estimated errors in focal length and tilt ranging from 0.01 to 0.1 degrees and 0.1 to 0.3 degrees, respectively. Furthermore, the method's error rate in estimated azimuth is significantly lower than that of estimated tilt. The proposed technique integrates seamlessly with existing feature-based stitching algorithms to produce high-quality stitching results, as demonstrated by experiments conducted on various datasets including those derived from smartphone, tablet, and panoramic images taken from a drone.

When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state can arise in such networks. We have conducted a detailed analysis on how this chimeric state is formed and stabilized in systems where the asynchronous elements outnumber the synchronous ones. Our research reveals that a specific threshold of asynchronous elements is required to create the chimeric state in such networks. Beyond this threshold, various chimeric patterns can emerge, and these patterns can be created and destroyed through the transformation of asynchronous elements into synchronous ones and vice versa. Moreover, when the chimeric state is established, it can exhibit a robust state, and an adjustment in parameters is required for its transformation.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from Pineau et al. (2003), our research focuses on the sample-efficient learning aspect. We investigate a modified maximum likelihood approach that integrates both state and action transitions within the model, learning an joint probability distribution between states and actions. We apply this distribution learning in the context of discrete action spaces for the Tabular setting, leveraging it for policy transfer and robust controller design. Our method is evaluated on various scenarios that deviate from the assumed environment model only in the probabilistic sense. Our results indicate that modeling the joint distribution of states and actions offers more accurate environmental representations compared to focusing solely on states.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, which is in line with a higher slice algebra. This type of algebra can be seen as part of a larger module category for which a Hall algebra and extended Frobenius-Katz correspondence exist. This connection to category modules also allows us to adapt and extend established methods for counting modules in a certain type of category, which in turn helps to achieve the same outcomes as a modified and extended version of Frobenius-Katz that applies across categories.

Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, a similar duality is demonstrated using random tensor networks.  By examining individual tensors, non-trivial effects are discovered that resolve discrepancies at the page phase transition.  By aggregating these effects, the reflected entanglement spectrum is derived analytically and aligns with numerical findings, providing a framework for resolving order of limits issues.  Applying this method to hyperbolic networks yields results consistent with holographic predictions.  Furthermore, a distinct entanglement structure and a non-hungarian phase in random tensor networks are observed, which can be related to a non-abelian anyon state and a gapped spectrum, respectively.

Even when external influences on a system are random, its internal organization can lead to lasting impacts on its behavior. In order to understand how heritable properties emerge from within a system, it is necessary to make distinctions between different types of information that a system may contain. For instance, information related to a system's robust, long-term characteristics varies significantly from the fluctuating patterns of randomness that surround its short-term fluctuations. In the context of a system's dynamics, this distinction corresponds to distinguishing between the shape of its underlying attractor and the random noise that surrounds it. 

In this paper, we define specific criteria that a system must meet in order for its patterns of organization to persist and influence its long-term behavior. Specifically, these criteria dictate that the probability of random fluctuations aligning with these patterns of organization must be relatively low, thus ensuring that the system's patterns of organization have a definitive, preferred orientation. In the context of a system's dynamics, this corresponds to the requirement that the system must have an attractor around which its random fluctuations must converge and organize themselves. 

These criteria that a system must meet in order for its patterns of organization to persist and influence its long-term behavior are seen to apply universally to all types of systems, regardless of whether they are in a state of steady or changing equilibrium. We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and non-invertible form. This model is of interest due to its simple construction, allowing for an intuitive understanding of its behavior. A notable aspect of this system is the emergence of attractors in the form of stable fixed points, cycles, and strange attractors. These attractors can be found through an analytical method that localizes them in relation to the control parameters. This method also enables the calculation of open topological boundaries, within which the 3D generalized H\'{e}hen map displays different dynamics. Furthermore, this approach reveals specific patterns in the behavior of the system's escape times and the dimensions of the attractors, all of which are confirmed by computational checks using a shooting technique.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept that links both scattering amplitudes and classical solutions, as well as suggesting its application to more complex, non-perturbative data. In the case of loop-based observables, the proposed duality results in a split interpretation, with one form involving a singular approach and the other a more intricate, higher-order expansion. Building upon previous theory first posited by Capovilla, Montero, and Reisenberger, the current paperwise content refines and solidifies the previously proposed loop equations for both singular and split interpretations. We analyze the statistical behavior of specific hook count distributions for Young tableaux that satisfy specific symmetry conditions. These counts are weighted towards younger tableaux with respect to a specific notion of "youth". The primary focus lies on the behavior at the edges of the Young shape, yielding two key probability distributions, $P_{2|n}$ and $P_{3|n}$. These distributions have already been studied for younger tableaux in a broader context by S. Shipman in reference [Ship09]. In our work, we derive the generating functions for the probabilities $P_{2|n}$ and $P_{3|n}$ that govern hook counts divisible by two and three, respectively, for hooks of size $k$. The deriving process involves expressing hooks in terms of chains and single-box subboxes.

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock displays two distinct times, including the standard quantum tunneling time and an alternative time influenced by spin fluctuations. The alternative time can be calculated using the Larmor clock's behavior and is related to the standard quantum tunneling time by an expression that accounts for spin fluctuations. The relationship between the two times remains valid even in complex spin systems. The validity of this relationship was confirmed through experiments involving a single electron and various nuclear particles. The alternative time can be utilized in experiments to modify the standard quantum tunneling time. The study also explores how to optimize spin fluctuations for their impact on tunneling. The alternative time can be utilized in two models - the transmission time model and the average force model. These models aim to define the force experienced by a particle as it tunnels through a potential barrier and can be studied using quantum systems with complex interactions. The study also discusses the potential applications and implications of these models and the alternative time in understanding particle interactions at the quantum level. The study further explores the modeling by deriving an expression for the average force based on particle energy and its momentum in a particular energy state. The alternative time can be studied in complex systems of interacting quantum particles and has been demonstrated in experiments involving various nuclear particles and a single electron. The study also explores the modeling of particle interactions and their influence on the alternative time and has been applied to understand particle interactions in complex systems of two particles

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function, irrespective of specific meson types. As an example, the amplitudes for P-wave charmonia mesons are studied, utilizing QCD sum rules to establish a model for the universal function specific to this meson type. Moreover, the research establishes connections between the moments of the universal function and the matrix elements controlling non-relativistic corrections in P-wave charmonia amplitudes. Our findings reveal that the characteristic magnitude of these relativistic corrections amounts to approximately thirty percent.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with the underlying quantum mechanical formalism. This study reimagines BEC dynamics using nonlinear unitary evolutions, framing all nonlinear effects as missing coherent control fields. This approach enables coherent control to mitigate these effects, maintaining consistency with the quantum mechanical formalism. Utilizing this understanding, a controlled phase shift gate has been developed and analyzed, with corresponding proposals for experimental realization.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate a closed symmetry algebra without a central extension or anomaly, whereas other research suggests that quantizing these charges results in a deformation when combined. This paper reexamines this problem considering updated understanding of superrotation charges and finds that quantization of eBMS charges within a new phase space, which includes a spin memory mode, leads to an algebra without a deformation. The degenerate vacua are characterized by the soft news and a Schwarzian mode corresponding to deformations of the celestial metric by superrotations. The calculation of eBMS charges is facilitated through a new thermal trace formula. The extended BMS algebra with its charges provides a quantum gravity interpretation of the extended double soft theorem recently discovered in string theory.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. The task becomes particularly demanding when models need to learn online, keeping the memory footprint small, and achieving a high performance from the very start. The recently introduced Online Ensemble Continual Learning (OECL) task and method offer a promising approach to addressing these issues. However, the problem with traditional methods is that they often require an initial data pass, hindering their ability to learn from the very start. In this research, a neural architecture called AArch-OECL has been designed specifically to tackle the OECL task. Our new approach combines an ensemble-based method with an architecture tailored for online learning. In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve applying Cartan's structure equations and generalizing them to explore new concepts. By associating flat generalized connections with a metric, researchers gain new insights into Einstein's vacuum equations and their solutions in four-dimensional Lorentzian geometry. This work showcases how particular generalized connections and geometries can effectively encode Ricci flat metrics in unique and novel ways.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The health risks associated with these infections cause a multitude
of issues, such as physical and mental disorders, often resulting in the death
of young children and immunocompromised individuals. Notwithstanding a propensity
for human diagnostic error, visual inspection is still predominantly utilized
for clinical diagnoses. Previous studies exploring the application of computer-
aided intestinal parasite classification have faced challenges due to the visual
similarities between parasites and other contaminants in fecal matter. This
paper introduces Deep Belief Networks as a solution to the challenges of
automatic intestinal parasite classification, presenting successful results from
three comprehensive datasets featuring images of eggs, larvae, and parasites/
eggs/larvae combinations. The proposed approach achieved an average accuracy of
$94.81\%$ with a database of 1,504 images, including a $96.15\%$ accuracy rate
when classifying larvae samples from a dataset of 1,296 images, and a $93.56\%$
accuracy rate for combined parasites/eggs/larvae in a dataset of 1,600 images.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve a resulting nonlinear integro-differential Bellman equation. An iterative procedure is developed to guarantee the convergence of the approximating sequence to the true Nash equilibrium. Notably, this approach can adapt to various reinsurance models with unique characteristics and offers the ability to estimate Nash-Sohl-Nash and Nash-Lindenberg-Tan models with regime-switching jump-diffusion models, featuring compound Poisson-type models. An illustrative numerical example demonstrates the method's effectiveness.

This research presents a novel proportional-integral-derivative-associative (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter and stochastic dual simplex algorithm (SDSA) for proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller tuning. The proposed PIDA controller is applied to a non-linear flight simulator model, enabling stable and smooth flight trajectories. Additionally, the integration of a genetic filter enhances the robustness of the control system and facilitates stable flight in various conditions. The efficacy of the proposed PIDA controller is demonstrated through multiple scenarios.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the cross section and phase volume being calculated to the required precision.
Key aspects of isospin symmetry in the pion-nucleon system are thoroughly explored.
Utilizing this analysis, the dispersion relation for the pion-nucleon amplitude is determined.
Also, the pion-nucleon scattering phase volume is evaluated through the method of construction.
From the dispersion relation, the pion-nucleon amplitude is analytically extended to its high-energy limit.
In conjunction with the calculated pion-nucleon scattering cross section, the required precision for the phase volume is established.
With charge symmetry applied, the pion-nucleon phase volume meets the necessary requirements for heavy nuclei and atomic energy applications.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it was later replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. In the upgraded variant, newly integrated forward pixel sensors were given enhanced responsibilities, utilizing novel readout schemes. Two such novel sensors, pilot blades, were introduced during a dedicated pilot experiment. In the analysis presented here, the development of the software used to reconstruct the tracks produced by these innovative forward pixel sensors is explored, with particular focus on identifying common challenges and incorporating relevant mitigation strategies.

We have developed a machine learning-based system to identify and categorize
the host galaxies of active galaxies within the redshift range of $z<1$ using
images from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey. Our study focuses on two types of
host galaxy morphologies: elliptical and spiral. Using elliptical and spiral
templates of varying sizes, we have created and trained k-nearest neighbor
classifiers to predict the likelihood of host galaxies belonging to each type.
Our predictions have an accuracy of 86.7% for elliptical and 85.7% for spiral
host galaxies. Next, we plan to apply this system to large datasets to gain
insights into the evolution of active galaxies over time.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations occur within the nucleus due to short-range correlations. In order to grasp the impact of these correlations, it's necessary to examine both their magnitude and spatial distribution. In this investigation, the relationships between the one-body density and the Wigner distribution of short-range correlations are explored, with the goal of delving into the spatial distribution of correlations affecting high-energy particles. Furthermore, the study analyzes the distribution of high-momentum fluctuations within different momentum states. Employing realistic simulations of a neutron gas tied to a mean-field potential, it is demonstrated that the spatial distribution of fluctuations corresponds directly to the momentum distribution. In particular, the region of low momentum with high energy and spatial spread primarily stems from the most extreme regions of the nucleus. Additionally, this effect is more pronounced in dense regions of the nucleus. The characteristics of high-momentum fluctuations at low momentum states were found to be closely linked to the overall density of the region in question.

We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its applications. By extending the complex domain without considering complex scaling, Deep Complex Networks (DCN) is limited in its ability to classify complex data based solely on argument. In this research, we present CN-SR, a method that applies scaling and rotation to modify the co-domain of classification models such as DCN, thereby enhancing their performance. CN-SR achieves this by mapping various CN models' outputs to a more optimal state, resulting in the model consistently predicting a fixed vector representing rotation only. CN-SR boasts an innovative concept resolving the classification paradox by utilizing its predictor to rectify phase discrepancy between input data and training labels, thereby eliminating the inherent problem inherent in complex number systems. CN-SR boasts a simplified design, achieving end-to-end training, and demonstrates significant improvements in performance over traditional CN models. CN-SR's effectiveness is showcased in its successful application on two common complex data classification tasks: circularly clustered data and complex electroencephalography signal classification.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  Once the gluon distribution reaches saturation, it establishes a distinctive gluon distribution shape characterized by a gluon rapidity density independent of initial conditions, resulting in various scaling phenomena observed in various processes.  This article will outline the theoretical foundation of the saturation phenomenon, followed by presentations of associated phenomenologies in ep scattering and heavy ion collisions, in addition to relevant experimental findings.

A thorough study measured the abundance of twelve key metal elements within 506 low-metallicity ($-1.6 \leq [Fe/H] \leq -0.3$) stars) in the Galactic bulge area, focusing on determining their gas cloud of origin. Ten of the elements are primarily formed through either big bang nucleosynthesis or stellar nucleosynthesis within low-metallicity environments. Abundance variations among gas clouds were determined and compared to theoretical models, revealing significant dispersion ranging from 0.03 to 0.30 dex. Abundance patterns indicated that most of the dispersion came from phosphate and aluminium production mechanisms. As a result, stars with low iron content but high phosphate levels were found to have lower gas temperatures of approximately 10,000K. In contrast, stars without low iron content but high phosphate levels were found to have higher gas temperatures of around 20,000K. Furthermore, the sample showed that iron abundance presented two distinct patterns, with one group having lower iron content but higher temperatures of around 20,000K and other with higher iron content but lower temperatures of around 10,000K.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of influential data points on predictions. The algorithm can be used with various machine learning models and will be a valuable tool for datasets containing a large number of features, such as health and financial data, where many relevant factors may exist. Initially tested on a synthetic dataset, the model demonstrated high accuracy and predictive stability. Furthermore, the approach was applied to real-world data from the Swiss Health Survey, where a regression tree ensemble was used to analyze and classify participants based on their health vocabulary and financial planning abilities. A local sensitivity analysis revealed that a small percentage of respondents tend to overrepresent specific financial literacy subgroups in predictions. Subsequent model adjustments were made to rectify overcompensation, resulting in improved overall performance and heightened sensitivity among minority groups.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how the choice of output affects the scalability of quantum models when utilizing gradient-based optimization.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in Sasakian manifolds. On the other hand, non-trivial semi-slant warped products have been discovered in cosymplectic manifolds, and several foundational results have been obtained, including a defining characteristic of such semi-slant warped products.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their strategy and reveals the existence of four stable states. A more in-depth analysis, incorporating colloid size and shape, shows various stable states, including antichemotactic dimers that follow specific patterns. These results provide valuable insights into the different survival techniques adopted by dimer configurations in various activity scenarios.

We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, contrasting them with the behavior observed in 1/3 states and those near half filling. Unlike those latter states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 each display magnetoroton spectral densities with two peaks rather than one, featuring magnetorotons with a spin of 2, whose chiralities differ for the 2/7 and 2/9 states, but share the same chirality in the 2/9 case. Our calculations also affirm the theoretical prediction that connects the guiding center spin with the spectral properties of the magnetorotons, and the predicted relationships among certain topologically distinct excitations, known as trion-hole and magnetoroton pairs, hold true, but display more complex relationships than initially proposed. Moreover, the results for various ν=1/m states indicate that the predicted relationships among these excitations do not generalize to other states near quarter filling.

Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing individuals into equitable subgroups to simplify the analysis, but a more inclusive approach is possible. Focusing on SIS epidemics, we present a geometric approach to determine the long-term probability distribution of finding the epidemic's growth status. Applying advanced mathematical tools enables us to relax the strict equiprobability assumption, allowing for varied probabilities of finding an individual infected within each subgroup. Moreover, containing an outbreak becomes a simpler target to optimize, as we can adjust the probabilities of individuals infected status within each subgroup.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results, but it's inherently biased in certain circumstances that cause 'x' in the data, leading to anomalous readings beyond the data's inherent limits. One specific scenario in which this occurs is when sampling a single process and applying data vector dimensions that don't accurately reflect its dimensions. This phenomenon can also manifest itself in the presence of instrumental biases that are not accounted for. Our research aims to explain the underlying mechanics of these 'x' anomalies and proposes a specific remedy for correcting them that's particularly effective in cases involving instrumental biases that are inherent in the instruments themselves.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through learning in goal-conditioned settings. Our research focuses on a simulated teaching environment where teachers instruct learners to achieve a goal by utilizing object attributes. We examine the learner's ability to adapt to a teacher's potentially ambiguous instructions by using object attributes. Our experiments reveal that incorporating referential ambiguity and tailor-instruction mechanisms significantly reduces the learner's task difficulty. Additionally, incorporating ambiguity-reducing mechanisms, such as aligning learner and teacher attribute preferences, greatly improves the learner's task efficiency. Our research demonstrates that aligning learner and teacher preferences leads to more efficient alignment with each other's preferences over time.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow state tomography to the forefront, addressing the challenge of process characterization and leveraging the CHSH inequality to derive simpler measurement sequences for process tomography via shadowing. This approach applies to both entirely quantum channels and combinations of quantum and classical channels involved in quantum information applications.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications systems. By harnessing their adaptability and swift deployment capabilities, it becomes feasible to supply content in densely populated areas or regions lacking essential infrastructure. Nevertheless, rapid energy depletion in UAVs restricts their operational range and necessitates continuous recharging. To address this limitation, it is vital to develop optimized strategies for repositioning the UAVs within a predetermined timeframe. This research aims to achieve a charging strategy that maximizes the UAV's trajectory efficiency. To that end, it proposes a two-step approach: obtaining an approximate trajectory through simulation and subsequently refining it using gradient-based optimization. The resulting trajectory is evaluated and compared to established methods across various scenarios.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. The presence of quadratic terms stems from a nearby resonance at higher energy. The removal of this resonance resonance by applying bias leads to a quadratic-to-linear transition at the bilayer's center, accompanied by a spontaneous symmetry breaking phenomenon, resulting in a spontaneously generated magnetic field. The use of the renormalization group (RG) method reveals that this symmetry breaking is due to an unsaturated fermion-fermion interaction caused by Coulomb repulsion. The application of RG method also uncovers other unsaturated instabilities, such as a charge density wave (CDW) in graphene monolayer and a Klein tunneling charge density wave (KT-CDW) in a structure composed of two graphene layers. The unsaturated nature of these instabilities implies that they occur even in the limit of vanishingly small bias voltage.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions. For Sc2TbN@C80, the conformation directly relates to the presence of an electric and a magnetic dipole moment. Theoretical studies indicate a highly temperature-dependent structure of Sc2TbN@C80 that transforms from an icosahedral to a prolate icosahedral structure above 300 K. The same research shows that this type of cluster @C80 exhibits a distinct herringbone pattern with a significant effect of the surrounding substrate on its orientation. The presence of an inhomogeneous substrate-induced force or anisotropy in the periodic force field of an inorganic substrate can potentially align or fix the orientation of Sc2TbN@C80. The superparamagnetic Tb-ion in Sc2TbN@C80 can be magnetically aligned by an external substrate, for example a graphite or h-BN substrate. The arrangement of Sc2TbN@C80 on an inorganic substrate influences both the conformation of the cluster and its potential to be aligned magnetically. The research also suggests that Sc2TbN@C80 or similar clusters can serve as microscopic sensors to detect changes in the chemical environment at room temperature. The conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 or similar clusters is highly responsive to external factors such as temperature, external magnetic fields, and the type of surrounding inorganic substrate. The internet of things encompasses diverse devices, ranging from domestic appliances to medical equipment and industrial sensors, which differ significantly in their operational environments, constraints, and functionalities.  These variations include devices' energy sources, energy efficiency, storage capacity, and computational power as well as their security requirements.  Various LoRaWAN security services such as encryption, decryption, authentication, and security association are offered, which involve key exchange for each service.  This study aims to evaluate the effect of using the same key for multiple services and proposes the implementation of a single key for multiple services to enhance security efficiency and reduce potential risks.  We examined the most widely used algorithms for each security service and analyzed their security shortcomings.  Ultimately, based on our findings, a single key was selected for multiple LoRaWWAN security services, which were tested and validated using the JUnit framework to ensure their proper functioning.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and we investigate its optimization through a sequential Bayesian experimental design that maximizes measurement precision. The model-based optimal-control algorithm used in this study generates pulse amplitudes optimally suited for various qubit models, including those influenced by noise and imperfect coherence. When pitted against an adaptive greedy algorithm in a series of measurements, our optimal-control method consistently yields higher precision at the expense of a small increase in uncertainty for certain noise scenarios. However, in cases with noise not accounted for by the model, both methods demonstrate similar asymptotic precision. Generally, our results indicate that optimal-control measurements offer greater precision in a wide range of scenarios, and the mechanisms enabling this outcome could also benefit other quantum measurement procedures.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at different scales based on the diameter of the shortest path tree, offering a seamless transition between extreme scales. It is demonstrated that this information-theoretic metric shares properties with other centrality measures and is applicable to various network types. A data analysis example demonstrates the ability of Gromov centrality to identify nodes with unique characteristics across multiple Boston housing datasets.

This paper introduces a novel, spherical and temporal theory of gravity that is based on an azimuthally symmetric field. It deviates from the traditional Newtonian concept of potential, instead employing a scalar quadrupole model for the gravitational field. The research establishes the fundamental equations of this theory, including its derivatives, provides an analysis of a particle's equation of motion, and proves the analogues of the Einstein's first law and Mercator's projection. Furthermore, it discusses the practical applications and constraints of this theory.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrices, a comparable study for matrix pencils remains in its early stages. To understand the critical differences between matrix and pencil bundles, consider that a matrix can be full-rank, whereas a pencil necessarily has a rank less than the number of columns. A recent finding reveals that most bundles of matrix pencils comprise infinitely many elements, and these bundles form continuous vector fields over specific spaces that are topologically equivalent to circles. Moreover, it has been found that the bundles of matrix pencils define fundamental groups within spaces that are topologically equivalent to spaces defined by bundles of matrices.

The mathematical concept of topological T-duality for an twisted torus is formulated, building upon the work of Bär and Große-Krüger. The near-horizon geometry of this setup is defined, and associations with string theory and topological T-duality are discussed. The paper also explores the isospectral property of the Laplacian in this context.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le established that any metric of tree width $w$ can be embedded in a $w^2$-treewidth graph. We expand on this by developing a more practical method for embedding metrics, one that requires a diameter-$d$ metric to be embedded in a $O(d)$-treewidth graph with minimal distortion. When applied to 3-spherical metrics, this yields a treewidth bound of $O(\sqrt{d})$. We further demonstrate that our approach allows for a minor-free minor-approximation with treewidth proportional to $\log(\frac{k}{\epsilon})/\log^{1-\epsilon}(k)$, a result that holds for any $k$-minor-free metrics.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values.

The potential of noise-tolerant variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), which employs intermediate quantum protocols, lies in its ability to utilize state-of-the-art quantum computers. To further enhance this approach, we introduce a modified VQE method, which converts a noisy protocol into a stable one by utilizing a different physical representation. Specifically, our adapted protocol uses the excitation of qubits instead of the standard computational basis. By doing so, we observe a significant decrease in the impact of depolarizing noise. Furthermore, we develop a technique to convert the excitation protocol into a stabilizer form without increasing circuit depth. Experimental results demonstrate that the adapted protocol outperforms the original one, achieving greater robustness to depolarizing noise for certain quantum hardware. Additionally, our study examines the effects of circuit complexity on both protocols.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping. This interaction becomes complicated in inference, rendering it challenging to utilize the learned representations in downstream tasks. To address this issue, we developed an approach called the deep generative decoder. It calculates the maximum likelihood estimates of the intermediate representations given some input data. The method can be viewed as an iterative process similar to the ones used for training, but applied in reverse. We examined two possible implementations of this approach, including a computationally efficient method that uses a hierarchical variational autoencoder. The efficacy of this method was tested on a mixture of Gaussian distributions and the latent space of a VAE-trained face data set. Furthermore, we employed the deep generative decoder to determine the underlying causes of a given set of representations, through the use of an inverse covariance matrix called the "basis chase." The approach was successfully applied to an analysis of a subset of test cases from the Pancreatic Cancer Expression Database, uncovering novel, previously unknown subtypes of pancreatic cancer.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be linked to hypothetical modulated sources or even an early universe phenomenon known as primordial stochastic gravitational waves generated during inflation. Research indicates that such waves, possibly amplified by an energy-dense state called the stiff phase, could explain both the observed frequency spectrum and amplitude of these modulated sources. We explore the possibility that the Stochastic Gravity Background, possibly stemming from inflation, is responsible for the NANOGrav findings and discuss its potential to resolve the long-standing Hubble tension in conjunction with cosmic inflation. Additionally, our analysis takes into consideration the existing limits from the Advanced LIGO-Virgo collaboration and possible future detections by future gravitational wave observatories.

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We analyzed Comet C/2015 ER61 using an Atacama Compact Array, which led to the discovery of molecular emissions, including H2O, CO, CS, CH3CN, and HCN. We found that CS, in particular, displayed unusual behavior in its spectral lines, suggesting the presence of a non-uniform source within the comet's 37 to 84 km radius shell. This discovery is significant as it challenges the traditional understanding of CS as originating from the nucleus' surface. Our findings from ER61 support the hypothesis that CS can be found in the comet's atmosphere when it originates from a more southern orbit. A comparison with data collected on Comet 41P/Solander in 2017 revealed differences in ER61's water to carbon ratio, as well as in the water to carbon monosulfide ratio, and in the abundance of certain molecules when the two comets were at similar distances from the sun. Finally, our analysis of ER61's data provided valuable information about its sublimation energy, and two potential models that describe ER61's gas production as it varied in distance from the sun.

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding.

This research explores Tsallis holographic dark energy in a modified quintessence approach, where the non-linear characteristics of the universe are more accurately represented. We examined two possible models, derived from constraints on the equation of state and calculation of the effective cosmological constant for the first model, second derivative methods were not needed as the equation of state resulted in a constant value. For the second model, the equation of state and deceleration parameter were determined to be dynamic in nature.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world optimizations. This type of problem often has a vast search space containing an abundance of local optima. The emergence of multi-objective algorithms designed for continuous domains has led to the generation of diverse and comprehensive non-dominated frontiers within these search spaces. This research introduces an enhanced version of the NSGAII algorithm, integrated with a branching scheme, designed to solve multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. The proposed algorithm, referred to as MO_NSGAII, utilizes a branching module to divide search spaces into manageable sub-domains, thereby optimizing computational efficiency. The efficacy of MO_NSGAII is demonstrated through experimental comparisons with four competing algorithms on a diverse set of test cases. The outcomes reveal MO_NSGAII to be the most efficient, capable of generating superior quality Pareto fronts with fewer function evaluations.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid.

The 2019 Data Fairness Workshop highlighted several critical challenges that must be addressed by the biomedical community to establish a safe and efficient data sharing framework. To tackle these challenges, we suggest a comprehensive solution approach, which focuses on the development of secure and robust data sharing platforms leveraging the power of cyberinfrastructure. To facilitate flexible and dynamic data sharing, these platforms should provide users with seamless access to a wide assortment of computational resources, extending beyond traditional data analysis capabilities to include agile and dynamic data management, scalable workflows, and cutting-edge tools for data protection. Here, we describe the design and functionality of two such data sharing platforms: Bioinformatics Knowledge and Cyberinfrastructure Gateway as well as the National Institute of Mental Health Research Domain Environment. We demonstrate how these platforms facilitate data management services including discovery, access, annotation, indexing, search, query, visualization, restoration, updating, and deletion. Furthermore, they enable sophisticated data analysis through the execution of computational workflows and offer a secure environment for sharing and executing applications, all while ensuring data protection via encryption, access control, and other security measures.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we utilize a supervised pre-training approach on extensive sentiment-annotated datasets drawn from relevant linguistic sources. By aligning implicit sentiment phrases with their matching sentiment labels, this method significantly improves its representation learning results. Consequently, our technique achieves an outstanding performance of 64.5% on the Google E-commerce dataset, a benchmark widely used in the field.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. Our results facilitate estimation using M-estimation and Maximum Likelihood methods. A simulation demonstrates the increased efficiency of the developed methods over weighting techniques in estimating outcome and mediator model parameters. We re-examine a German dataset to determine whether reduced immunocompetence impacts the likelihood of listeriosis through the use of gastric acid suppressors.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS element limitations.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two simpler subproblems and apply the block coordinate descent approach to iteratively solve for these subproblems using the blockwise linearization and approximation of the weighted minimum secrecy rate function.
Our results from numerical tests demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing solutions.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through review and efficient relabeling. To achieve this, we introduce an optimal strategy where the value of each perception is matched with the corresponding class label to create a valuable memory database with associated rules. This process is then used to train an efficient counter-measure network that can counter an evolving class of threats by matching unlabelled new data with the existing labelled data through contrastive learning. Although the initial tests showed promising results for this theory, it also brought its own set of challenges that needed to be addressed.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of the solar wind. We compared our findings with data from the Ulysses mission near the poles of the sun and from the Helios 2 helmet, and we also used predictions from a model that simulates the solar wind. We compared the energy flux at the Ulysses and Helios 2 missions with their corresponding observation distances from the solar center, and we also compared the energy flux at the Parker Solar Probe with the predictions from the model, however we noticed a significant difference in the energy flux at the PSS, and we observed that the energy flux at its closest approaches did not match the expected values from the model, and we attributed this discrepancy to the discovery that the solar wind energy typically reaches its maximum at a distance from the sun that is more than the closest approaches of the PSS, and we suggested that the solar wind energy peaks at a distance that corresponds approximately to the end of its observation period, and we proposed that the solar wind energy significantly increases as it leaves this area, and we provided evidence of

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves defining a locally trivial G-C*-algebra, which represents the local version of a noncommutative numerable principal bundle. When the space G acts freely and properly on A, the resulting local triviality manifests as (G,x) being inner, and we derive a universality property for this G-C*-algebra. Building upon this framework, we explore relationships between functors associated with C*-algebra bundles and examine examples, including those derived from noncommutative projective geometry's sphere bundles.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of $P$-points. Using this finding, we establish that it is possible in a specific set of circumstances that the first uncountable ordinal is less than the least size of a maximal almost-disjoint family, yet the least size of a maximal antichain of uncountable cardinals is greater than the former. Furthermore, we derive an upper limit on the size of a maximal almost-disjoint family that can be constructed through the least size of a maximal antichain of uncountable cardinals of size $\aleph_1$.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives the exploration of these systems in this research, where theoretical models are developed for $q$-deformed optomechanical systems featuring two types of nonlinearities. Specifically, these models involve linear and nonlinear interactions within a cavity and coupling between the cavity and a mechanical resonator. By solving the eigenvalue equation, the spectra of these systems are examined, yielding insights that $q$-deformation facilitates the creation of optomechanical double-well potentials and adjusts light group velocities. Moreover, $q$-deformation enables the production of infinite optical band gaps and regulates the phase and amplitude of optical non-reciprocity. Crucially, $q$-deformation can either diminish or enhance light group velocities and tunneling times, contingent on the choice of parameters, including the deformation parameter, mechanical coupling, and nonlinear interactions. This investigation not only delves into the physical aspects of $q$-deformed optomechanical systems but also unlocks their potential for manipulating and understanding optical phenomena.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the symmetry plane of the system, showing its consistency across different nuclear shapes. Research then focused on calculating reflection operators for the quantum two-rotor system, enabling the derivation of Hamiltonians for negative scissors states with reflections and their counterparts with gauge invariance. Lastly, I investigated the relationship between these states and local ripples.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to approximate fluxes, thereby enabling the computation of solutions with the finite volume framework. This approach proves effective for both hyperbolic and parabolic PDEs, as demonstrated through theoretical convergence analysis. Furthermore, the mentioned research reveals that the novel method shares similarities with existing numerical techniques while offering an artificial neural network based alternative to traditional schemes.

The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, studies on the experiment's future are underway, with the primary goal being to establish a dedicated heavy-ion program following Run 3. This effort focuses on exploring two possible paths: 1) enhancing the ALICE detector-end equipment and 2) establishing a new experiment within the LHC. In the first case, planned upgrades include replacing the current central barrel detectors with more advanced models and incorporating a new TRT tracker. In contrast, the second path involves collaborating with other LHC experiments or allocating new time slots on the LHC, although these options have yet to yield concrete outcomes. Despite these developments, work on the future ALICE strategy continues, with the experiment set to participate in the LHC Run 3 data collection and contribute to the research program.

The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase arising from this time-related entanglement between the future and past, showing that it can be quantitatively represented on a 2D space-time diagram. This geometric phase is analogous to the Aharonov-Bohm effect and can be attributed to an analogue of the electromagnetic vector potential. We propose that the geometric phase provides a viable means for detecting the Unruh effect through experiments designed to detect the Aharonov-Bohm effect.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for model development and evaluation. To fill this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset featuring detailed annotation for over 50,000 event occurrences in eight diverse languages. This resource not only covers entities but also accurately marks the events and associated elements, enabling further analysis of multilingual event extraction through thorough experimentation.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for Griffiths semipositive vector bundles, thus partially supporting Griffiths' conjecture on characteristic forms of positive characteristic.

Observations from the Neutron star Interior X-ray Event (NICXIE) telescope on board the AstroSat satellite have enabled researchers to analyze Cyg X-1, a high-mass black hole, using both direct and indirect analysis methods. As the star passes through the field of view, multiple spectra are collected using the medium- and hard-band detectors. For the first time, researchers are utilizing the stellar wind's momentum distribution, rather than relying on simplified assumptions. By applying this approach to the high state observations of Cyg X-1, both direct and indirect analysis yield comparable outcomes. The impact of the stellar wind on the model is analyzed using momentum distribution fitting parameters. Additionally, the momentum distribution's effect on timing analysis is evaluated by examining the fast Fourier transfer spectrum and light curves. The outcome shows that the stellar wind generates an artificial 'orbital' component in the fast Fourier transfer spectrum below a 1 Hz frequency, with an amplitude that surpasses the wind's overall signal by a factor of 10. The observed variability could be the result of the stellar wind interacting with the accretion disk. For the first time, researchers are utilizing the stellar wind's distribution in momentum rather than simplified assumptions. The momentum distribution of the hard state observations of Cyg X-1, the first set of data analyzed using this method, demonstrates consistency with the observed variability.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting findings in cognitive science that suggest humans simultaneously analyze both to understand sentence meaning. To address this disparity, this study examines how well the combination of two advanced parsing models, one focusing on syntax and one on semantics, can replicate the results of a single combined parser. The experiment uses a rich dataset containing detailed analyses of multiple types of sentence structure and finds significant improvements in accuracy when combining two models over running them separately. The joint parser was compared to two leading parsing systems, one syntax-based and one semantics-based, on multiple evaluation sets, and demonstrated substantial accuracy gains of up to 5.3 and 6.4 respectively.

The formation of magnetically driven winds and outflows from the remnants of binary neutron star or neutron star-black hole mergers significantly impact the amount of kilonova ejecta and the distribution of gold across the universe. The role of the accretion disk in these events has typically been assumed to be neutral or even diminishing the formation of outflows. In order to verify previous research findings, we utilized a 2D magnetohydrodynamic simulation to investigate how winds form on a neutrino-cooled, magnetically active disk. The simulation revealed that the disk itself generates a persistent, large-scale magnetosphere that forms a thin layer of gas. The simulation simulations show that this disk layer contributes a small amount of mass compared to the initial merger disk, but may be comparable to the mass of the magnetically driven wind. The creation of this structure does not appear to hinder the formation of magnetically driven outflows; therefore, we do not observe a significant reduction in the amount of outflow gas. The outflow rates remain largely unchanged from the initial merger scenario, with approximately $2\times10^{-3}M_{\odot}$. The outflow is comprised of two components, with the first component formed early on through disk wind formation and the second component formed through a nonradiative, magnetized disk. The outflow will have a low metal content but high isotropic element abundance due to the nucleosynthesis of these elements. The outflow may impact the surrounding environment and affect

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 E/S0 galaxies in our sample exhibited distinct tidal features, with a small percentage (2 percent) of these surrounded by two or more such structures. Through a logistic regression analysis, we found no correlation between tidal features and environmental settings. Our results imply a tidal feature removal rate of approximately 37 percent over the lifetime of these galaxies. Our study further suggests that tidal features are most commonly associated with galaxies of massive proportions, with a merger rate of around 0.14 per 500 million years for galaxies of 10 to the power of 11 solar masses. This rate of removal is consistent with findings from hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy interactions.

This paper is a component of a research series exploring the Theory of Gravitation with Repulsive Forces and its implications on the cosmos. Previously, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) was developed, demonstrating its ability to replicate the behavior of observed galaxy shapes, including spiral arms and central bars. Building on this foundation, the model is applied to a disk-shaped star system, predicting a radial force that can counteract the centrifugal effect in outer regions and lead to ejection in extreme areas, a phenomenon observed in nature.
