By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for virtual avatars, we
developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that uses DNR as its base.
ANR introduces two key components: a mesh image optimizer that aligns pre-rendered
meshes with input avatar data and accounts for camera perspectives, and a mesh-
conditioned DNR layer that uses the aligned meshes to produce high-quality images.
Using our approach, we can render realistic avatar images from arbitrary camera
angles without requiring pre-synchronized data, making it well-suited for a range of
applications, including real-time video streaming and augmented reality experiences.
To showcase the effectiveness of our method, we have presented several demonstration
videos featuring high-quality avatar images, available at the provided website.

Recent research indicates that deep learning models struggle with "adversarial" alterations that humans readily identify, prompting speculation that these models lack robust fundamental understanding. To investigate further, this study assesses how both humans and deep learning models react to various degrees of image transformations using a large dataset. The findings from this analysis suggest that both humans and deep learning models exhibit different responses to these transformations, with more extreme variations being easily detected by both but less so by shallow neural networks. This study also explores the implications of these findings, with results indicating that both humans and deep learning models exhibit similar tendencies in their reactions to these transformations. The data from this analysis is available at https://github.com/google-ml-images/transform-impact.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangle diagrams associated with three-strand braid groups that involve reflections are found to generate a basis for the space of Chern-Simons form on a specific torus-based manifold when specified conditions are met. Within this form, the eigenvalues of the AW algebra, along with their corresponding eigenvectors, are identified, which are found to be related to the quantum numbers $\ell+1$ and $m$. This research extends to 3D spheres by developing a global form of Chern-Simons form, which is also expressed in terms of the AW algebra operators.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation method, applied to two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets with weak inter-trimer interactions. Specifically, we investigate the ground state properties of Kitaev and Kitaev-Heisenberg models defined on a hexagonal lattice structure composed of evenly spaced sites. By employing a systematic finite-size analysis across various lattice sizes, our results confirm that the dominant effect in the weakly-coupled regime resides in the inter-trimer interactions, rather than the Kitaev frustration within individual clusters. Furthermore, for larger cluster spacings, a comprehensive phase diagram is predicted, showing an emergence of an extensive spin liquid state, bounded by ordered magnetic phases derived from classical ground states. Such behavior is also found in a related family of models involving strongly-coupled Kitaev-Heisenberg models. Our approach is found to yield accurate agreement with analytical solutions, ground-state quantum many-body wave functions, computations and classical simulations. Such correspondence holds across a broad range of model parameters.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by prompting them with reviews paired with labels such as "Does the user like this movie?" The model can then be trained to select "yes" or "no" from the subsequent word choices. However, optimizing the zero-shot objective is hindered by the pre-existing training objectives. To improve upon this limitation, researchers have proposed "meta-tuning" - directly fine-tuning pre-trained language models on aggregated datasets to optimize zero-shot performance. In this study, researchers focused on classification tasks and compiled a 43-dataset meta-collection with 188 labeled descriptions. When evaluated on new tasks, models optimized through meta-tuning demonstrated superior performance relative to their pre-trained counterparts, achieving up to a 7.3% improvement in accuracy. Notably, meta-tuning was relatively efficient, requiring significantly less training data and iterations than the pre-training process. The proposed dataset and prompt collection are accessible through public repositories at https://github.com/alevien/zeroshot-collection and https://github.com/alevien/metatuning-collection respectively.

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a electroweak phase transition in the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM is conducted. A vast portion of the model's parameter space investigated is consistent with multiple constraints. It is demonstrated that the LSP nature holds firm during the phase transition in the vast majority of parameters studied. These findings reveal that the LSP is composed of a light Higgs boson and one or two next lightest stable particles with masses less than or equal to 300 GeV. The research also suggests that the LSP is unlikely to be detected in future high-precision Higgs rate measurements. The possibility of detecting gravitational waves resulting from the phase transition in the NMSSM is explored via a parameterized approach, and it is found that a significant portion of the model's parameter space falls within a realistic detection range for the LISA telescope. A study of the phase transition and dark matter searches reveals that the LSP is composed of a Higgsino-like and a Wimp-like component. The research also suggests that the LSP is unlikely to be completely stable in certain scenarios involving rapid changes and high temperatures during the phase transition. The implications of these findings are that future gravitational wave detectors may be able to distinguish between NMSSM models with first or second order phase transitions, while early dark matter detection may be able to either rules out or leaves open the possibility of electroweak phase transitions.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying and verifying redshifts through both ATPN-C (atmospheric transmission in spectrum-corrected wavelength space) and spectrum analysis. Our approach involves generating pseudo-redshift ATPN-C spectra and spectra given a source redshift, matched to the capabilities of a specific instrument, allowing for the identification of redundant and non-redundant redshift estimates. Instrument characteristics that produce distinct ATPN-C spectra, such as ALMA, NOEMA, or IRAM, are used to simulate how the source appears under various conditions. This method proves effective in identifying and verifying multiple strong redshifts (z > 4) associated with ATPN-C data from LMT-NOEMA. Furthermore, we provide ATPN-C spectra for 51 galaxies studied by Manohar et al. (2021), allowing for the identification and verification of potential redshifts via visualization.

The dynamical properties of triangular lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnets with $S=1/2$ have been studied through nonmagnetic dilution in the form of random spin sites. At the critical point with 12.5% dilution, the dynamic structure factor shows clear distinctions between ordered and disordered phases. Upon thermal excitation, the spin-1 particles exhibit an energy gap $\Delta$, and their movement within the spin liquid environment generates a low-energy continuum. The low-energy continuum's intensity is directly correlated with the spin-1 particle density and its scale can be related to the spin susceptibility. The spin-1 particles' quadratic dispersiveness at $q=0$ influences the spin wave density of states, thereby explaining the observed density of states features. The density of states, spin excitation energy spectra, and dynamic structure factor analyses reveal a direct relationship with the spin-1 particle density. The experimental findings are compared with the findings from a Monte-Carlo model of 120-degree spin ordering on a triangular lattice.

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on symmetry breaking and gauge deconfinement through lattice simulations. The research involves varying the lattice gauge group while keeping the Higgs field transformations unchanged. The impact of lattice cutoff on the phase transition is examined by computing critical exponents and logarithmic disparities between free and interacting theories. The study also evaluates the standard mean-field approximation in four dimensions and compares results with previous studies in three dimensions.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in the study of antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its in-plane N\'{e}el vector at 300 K. This letter presents the results of neutron diffraction and specific heat measurements, as well as first-principles and Heisenberg spin-model calculations, to determine the in-plane magnetic structure and exchange interactions of Cr$_2$Al. The studies reveal a $B2$/tet $\rightarrow$ $DO19$/tet phase transition at 178 K. Exchanges were estimated to be within the ranges of $J_1$ = (23 $\pm$ 5) meV, $J_2$ = (7 $\pm$ 2) meV, $J_3$ = (1 $\pm$ 1) meV, and $J_4$ = $(0.2\pm0.1)$ meV with interstitial and interplanar exchange interactions. Heisenberg spin-model simulations, incorporating the 2nd nearest neighbor exchange interactions ($J_2$ = 7 meV), accurately explained the in-plane magnetic structure observed in Cr$_2$Al.

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating essential collision characteristics from Boltzmann's equation, while also reflecting the influence of the target velocity distribution function, akin to the Shakhov model. Following numerical simulations of strong non-equilibrium shock waves, a combination of theoretical and empirical methods is employed to develop a suitable velocity-dependent collision frequency for varying intermolecular potentials. As a result, the $
u$-model exhibits notable improvements in accuracy, along with a thorough examination of the developed velocity-dependent collision frequencies.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa, rely on a capability called semantic parsing. This parsing capability interprets the meaning of input natural language into a logical representation of its significance. This logical representation can then be utilized to retrieve relevant information from a database and provide responses to queries. However, developing semantic parsing capabilities is an intricate and resource-intensive process. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring new approaches. One recent breakthrough involves training semantic parsing models directly from existing logical databases and natural language examples. However, these models require a substantial amount of training data, consisting of both logical representations and natural language phrases, to be effective. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed an innovative training technique that only requires a small set of annotated natural language examples. This technique integrates logical rules and linguistic models to generate possible semantic representations for the input data. By training on these representations, the model can achieve exceptional parsing performance, even when provided with limited data. In fact, experiments have demonstrated that the model can learn to parse logical expressions from a database with only a few hundred annotated examples. This achievement showcases a significant breakthrough in semantic parsing research.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to gain a deeper understanding of how matter is formed. To achieve this goal, researchers are working on developing a forward silicon detector, known as fDST, as part of the EIC's detector design. To guarantee that the EIC lives up to its promise of furthering our knowledge of QCD, it's essential to include advanced forward detectors to collect data from distant interaction points, thereby enabling the detection of deeply inelastic scattering events, even those occurring at extremely low values of x and Bjorken-x. In the case of electron-proton collisions, these low values are accessible through certain kinematic conditions, but not in others. However, the situation changes for electron-nucleus collisions, as precise calculations indicate the existence of accessible regions across all possible kinematics. To confirm these predictions, researchers must design a forward silicon detector as part of the EIC's detector layout. To test its effectiveness, researchers have created simulated data models of forward events, even extreme ones, such as a low x and Bjorken-x event resulting from a deeply inelastic scattering process. Using this information, researchers can confirm that the EIC, equipped with its forward silicon detector, can collect essential data on deeply inelastic scattering events, thereby contributing to our understanding of QCD.

A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four low-mass active galactic nuclei (AGN) with masses similar to that of the Milky Way, made using the XMM-Newton space observatory, reveals the emergence of quasi-periodic oscillations lasting for a short duration of 10-50 seconds. The spectral analysis of these oscillations, observed within an energy range of 0.3-10 keV, failed to yield any distinct changes in their characteristics. There are two plausible explanations for these oscillations, with one being a phenomenon related to the accretion process near the event horizon of supermassive black holes, and another potentially linked to a burst of thermal energy. The likelihood of the oscillations being of a persistent nature is difficult to assess, and observations of these sources using future wide-field X-ray surveys with highly sensitive observatories may be able to confirm this hypothesis.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research aims to understand how these magnetic fields develop and how they impact a star's atmosphere. We examined HD58260, a silicon-type chromosphere star located about 300 light-years away, using spectro-polarimetry. Our analysis focused on calcium lines to uncover the balance between the magnetic field's influence and other atmospheric factors. The results show that the strength of the magnetic field varies significantly with the distance from the star's center. The higher-altitude regions exhibit weaker fields, a pattern opposite of expectations. The observed shift is quite large, with a difference of 500 Gauss between the outer and middle layers. The mechanism behind this unusual gradient is still unclear and needs further investigation to be confirmed. The discovery challenges current theories of the behavior of magnetic fields in stars.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's H30α self-absorption technique, researchers measured the molecular gas mass and star formation rate of NGC5253 using two different methods and compared the results with existing photometric estimates. The observed variability suggests that early type stars are forming at varying rates within the galaxy. An estimate based on Hα and far-infrared fluxes indicates a high star formation rate, but millimeter-wave observations of NGC5253 suggest that the galaxy's metallicity is around one tenth of that of the Milky Way. By comparing the galaxy's observations to those of other low-metallicity galaxies with similar star formation rates, researchers found the H30α method is as accurate or more accurate than other methods in measuring molecular gas mass and star formation rates. The study further indicates that the H30α method is a viable alternative for measuring these parameters in nearby galaxies.

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. Utilizing techniques from empirical operator approximation and operator smoothing, we derive rates of convergence for $[Pf](x)$ in relation to the Hilbert-Schmidt norm for any conditional expectation $P$. Our findings are applied to the case of Poisson regression, yielding practical implications and offering an alternative method to traditional parametric approaches for continuous design variables.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This paper creates observers for two distinct epidemic models, focusing on state estimation for partial information systems including unknown state variables. It proposes a novel differential equation to estimate the unknown state, incorporating an adjustment to compensate for errors. We establish theoretical proofs of stability and error convergence for both observers, demonstrating that actual estimation errors are bounded by a constant linked to the time derivative of the estimation error. Numerical simulations demonstrate the observers' ability to accurately track and converge to system states, achieving satisfactory performance in real-world scenarios.

The consideration of temporal aspects within knowledge graph embeddings has become increasingly significant. Current approaches aiming to capture temporal dynamics in models often overlook the fact that many real-world knowledge graphs themselves don't have a built-in temporal dimension. Since existing static models can effectively learn node representations, we explore the potential of adapting these models to address link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs by creating negative samples based on temporal edge absence. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that combining temporal and static model approaches to negative sampling offers superior performance.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has them mostly in an unstable resonator configuration, though there's still confusion about the inner working of KL mode-locking. The usual mathematical description relies on ABCD imaging parameters from stable resonator design, but this approach is flawed because KL mode-locking doesn't fit the criteria for ABCD matrices. Despite this issue, KL mode-locking has been mostly treated using conventional stable resonator methods. In this study, we revisit the KL mode-locking mechanism and develop a new, correct mathematical description that expands upon earlier work. The new description helps overcome limitations in combining high pulse energy with wide bandwidth, a challenge due to pulse energy loss in conventional KL resonator configurations. The correct mathematical description also allows for simulating pulse dynamics in a more accurate way, which is crucial for pulse choice and oscillator design.

Several recent studies have highlighted the potential of online federated learning (OFL) for distributed model training. Nevertheless, existing OFL research often overlooks two critical factors - the variability in data quantity across participating nodes and the non-linear regression task itself. These omissions can impede the success of OFL in real-world scenarios. In our research, we address these challenges through a novel asynchronous OFL framework that adapts to varying data quantities and utilizes a global average aggregation strategy with improved fictitious playing for enhancedregression performance. Offered a fixed communication budget, our proposed framework, called Normadis-OFL, outperforms traditional linear regression methods in the meta-Federated Learning benchmark, achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art non-linear regression methods while showcasing robustness across disparate communication budget scenarios.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, researchers investigate a back reflector with a nanostructured 3D photonic band gap crystal made from silicon that can easily be integrated into the existing thin films.  Using computational methods, the team simulates absorption in thin films with truncated crystal structures and compares them to perfect silicon films under various conditions.  Without compromising the overall spectral response, the team finds that employing a 3D photonic band gap crystal reflector can enhance the absorption of thin films by 25%, with potential for even greater improvements in thicker films.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. These functions are linked to nested exponentials through a useful functional equation and have a series representation that converges within a certain region of the complex plane. By examining the properties of $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, we can study the dynamics of exponential maps and obtain insights into the nature of solutions to the tetration equation, particularly in relation to Schottky groups and the boundary of the region of convergence.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but currently, direct constructions are limited to very few examples. Our method employs a simplicial complex built from an expander graph and groups of uniformly distributed random vertices, creating a new high dimensional expander for a specified dimension, giving designers a range of options for creating sets of random high dimensional expanders. Notably, this approach allows us to achieve certain statistical guarantees about our constructions. For lower dimensions (up to 8), we can showcase a significant deviation from previous constructions in terms of spectral properties. Our method also allows us to create various types of high dimensional expanders, each with distinct features and covering numbers. Additionally, we explored the relationship between our constructions and probabilistic tools, specifically, high dimensional analogues of coupon-collectors and the Erdos-Turán hypothesis. This research marks the first application of covering spaces in the field of high dimensional expanders.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A unique phase transition from a high-temperature, disordered state to a lower-temperature, ordered state with a magnetic structure that deviates from the expected by lattice geometry is observed. Further investigation revealed that the local magnetic interactions between Gd3+ ions are best explained by a 3D Heisenberg model, supporting the presence of a quasi-2D, honeycomb lattice of Gd ions. This discovery is consistent with theoretical predictions of a magnetic structure that exhibits a low-temperature order. Researchers also conducted a detailed analysis of the magnetic anomalies within the ordered state at 2K.

The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown remarkable success, but most real-world networks are sparse, which are currently underserved by this field. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) before passing it through a neural network for a dimensionally-reduced representation. Notably, our model generates this representation without altering the network's original structure. We tested the SSNE model using synthetic and actual sparse networks and found that it outperforms existing models in predicting links, which we demonstrated using predictions on specific networks. Overall, our model successfully addresses the challenge of developing effective node representations for link prediction in sparse networks.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 200 micrometer deep etch beyond conventional limits, enabling the creation of a large 200 micrometer deep silicon cell even with a starting chip thickness of only 50 micrometers. This allows for the production of 200 micrometer deep silicon cells with minimal loss due to photon scattering, optimal trapping conditions for alkali metals, and high visibility using a 1064 nanometer laser. As a result, we can attain a long 23 millisecond Ramsey interval for cesium, sufficient for single atom detection with high accuracy and without convolution from noise sources, such as the photodetector's response. Additionally, we can achieve atoms within the center of the cell using a 2 watt laser with an 8 millimeter long vapor chamber, powered by an external heat reservoir.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property damage, and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thus offering superior performance and reduced costs compared to traditional methods. Although traditional multi-spectral fusion techniques are widely available, they tend to struggle with identifying extended wildfire patterns. To overcome this limitation, we have developed FIRe-GAN, a novel deep learning-based approach for infrared-visible image fusion aimed at improving the overall performance of wildfire detection. To achieve this goal, FIRe-GAN employs a innovative hybrid training strategy combining paired and unpaired infrared-visible image pairs, thus enabling the network to retain detailed infrared data while capturing new infrared-visible features. Moreover, it utilizes a paired infrared-visible image domain translation network to enable the exchange of infrared and visible image domains. Our experiments, conducted using a newly-established benchmark dataset consisting of 20,000 images, have shown that FIRe-GAN outperforms state-of-the-art multi-spectral fusion approaches in terms of both overall accuracy and mean intersection over union, thus showcasing its potential as a cutting-edge deep learning-based infrared-visible image fusion technique for wildfire detection.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe complications.
Given the increasing demand for mental health services, leveraging technology to identify depression symptoms has become more feasible. Analyzing social media data poses an attractive option for mental health diagnostics, given its vast amount of user-generated content that often details their emotional state. However, standard machine learning methods face significant challenges when applying this data to make informed predictions about human behavior. To overcome these difficulties, developing accurate models of depression from social media data requires extensive training datasets and a deep understanding of depression as a mental disorder. By integrating psychological theories about depression into our models, we can achieve better outcomes in this field. To contribute to this goal, a dataset containing 1872 social media posts from individuals with depression and a larger group without it was collected and made available for research. To test and validate various machine learning algorithms, a comparison of five approaches was conducted using this dataset, which yielded impressive results. A practical implementation of a naive Bayes classifier demonstrated impressive accuracy and precision in detecting depression, offering significant potential for mental health interventions. By combining our dataset with a real-world system for identifying depression, we can offer users a choice to anonymously donate their social media data to aid in depression research, fostering a more collaborative environment. By advancing data-driven solutions to mental health issues, we can develop more effective treatments and support individuals with depression.

We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, calculating the time it takes for the number of infections to reach a certain threshold. We've also compared our findings to the actual course of the pandemic in South Korea, establishing a correlation between our predicted model and the actual outcome. Knowing when the number of infections reaches a threshold is crucial, as it indicates the point at which the pandemic is under control. We've established a practical method for making predictions based on our model, showing that early interventions are essential in reducing the spread of future pandemics.

The ISGMR and a low-lying quadrupole component, derived from the coupling of two main strength functions related to isoscalar monopole and quadrupole invariance, were studied using total reaction cross sections of $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si with various projectiles. By separating the two components based on energy dependence, the researchers were able to determine the ISGMR parameters and strength from combined data sets. This approach provided improved root-mean-square radii and energy centroids compared to previous studies. The results indicated reduced root-mean-square radii and higher energy centroids with increasing neutron number. The strength of the ISGMR was found to be higher in $^{28}$Si compared to $^{24}$Mg, and the decrease in strength was more pronounced in the silicon isotope. The increase in neutron number led to a decrease in ISGMR energy centroid.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse examples of convergence.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities. The approach employs an actor-critic Bellman equation to optimize portfolio settings across multiple securities. Training via Monte Carlo methods enables the acquisition of a policy optimization function, which can be used in subsequent applications with real-time data. The model's initial testing on synthetic markets and historical data revealed that it effectively hedges options when compared to benchmarks, including both theoretical models and more advanced deep learning methods.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their comprehensive historical interaction data. This data may indicate varied levels of user intent. For instance, reciting a public institution's listing of services might not represent strong user intent compared to signing up for those services. Existing sequential models are designed to address a recommender system's primary goal of making item suggestions, but they fail to account for variations in user intent. This distinction has significant implications for user experience and business goals. For instance, in cases where user intent is unclear (e.g., users ending up on a website without knowing how they got there), companies might want to switch to non-intrusive approaches (e.g., prompting users to sign up via text message). To address these issues, this research proposes a probabilistic framework for modeling user intent. This approach builds on user interaction data, intent modeling, and explicit user identification to provide a solid user intent framework grounded in user experience principles. To achieve this, the research introduces a probabilistic user intent modeling approach, incorporating latent user intent factors into a variety of established sequential recommendation models. Experimental findings on a large Yandex dataset show that by considering user intent variability, the integrated models outperform standalone sequential models.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out as a special instance of a general unfolding of a nilpotent vector field, specifically a Horn type vector field, which originates from the Lie algebra $sp_4(\mathbb{C})$. This derivation utilizes the nilpotent $sp_4(\mathbb{C})$-orbit under upper-triangular matrices representing the algebraic structure of the unfolding's singularity classification. Furthermore, key properties of the DCHE are examined within the context of its connection to the nilpotent origin unfolding.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues arise across various fields including statistics, computer science, and imaging sciences, with the task of estimating a low-rank matrix from noisy observations frequently involved. Past research has primarily focused on analyzing recovery performance in cases of identical measurement noise. Our work aims to expand this knowledge by studying the statistical limits of low-rank matrix recovery in more general scenarios where rows of the matrix are grouped based on varying levels of measurement noise. This is particularly relevant in imaging applications such as compressed sensing of natural language, super-resolution, and computational imaging. To achieve this goal, we introduce a new concept of joint measurability and its associated information-maximization framework, which enables us to fundementally limit performance in diverse rank-one estimation scenarios when faced with differently scaled measurement noise. Specifically, we develop exact joint reconstruction mutual information values for Gaussian and logistic models and develop high-level testing curves for general models. Furthermore, our results reveal that in cases of identical or uniformly scaled noise, the fundamental limits are unaffected and recover previously derived results, including those by Chen and Wainwright and Martinsson et al. from a different perspective.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is found to survive without symmetry, namely the relationship between bulk and edge dispersions.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value, $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$, is observed.

This study presents an approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is non-interactive and relies solely on its local output measurements. Importantly, new decoder designs enable controllers to be implemented without requiring global knowledge, thus facilitating seamless module addition and removal without recalibration, a crucial aspect for controller stability and performance. By distributing control authority effectively, the proposed design also achieves stability despite the decoupling of outputs and inputs through decoder transformations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT to capture the deeper-level context. The combination of these two components serves as input for a pre-trained BERT model that functions as a dual transformer, one for identifying lung infection and another for COVID-19 diagnosis. This approach achieved impressive results, with a 97% accuracy in detecting lung infection and an 85% accuracy in diagnosing COVID-19.

Network science is an rapidly growing field with numerous applications across biology, sociology, physics, epidemiology, neuroscience, computer science, and other disciplines. Recognizing its pivotal role in understanding various real-world phenomena, this field has expanded exponentially over the past two decades. As a result, an overwhelming amount of scientific data and tools now require expert filtering to separate crucial information from trivial discoveries. To provide a sense of direction and help navigate this complex field, this paper introduces the Resource Atlas for Network Science, offering a comprehensive framework to guide researchers in addressing pressing challenges. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, we will present real-world examples of applying Resource Atlases to three critical problems: (i) developing a universal language to describe brain cell networks, (ii) detecting hidden communities in network demand, and (iii) defining a computational framework to model supply and transport networks. By offering this framework, we aim to facilitate breakthroughs and discoveries in various areas of network science.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being increasingly used to describe the complex interactions between ecology and evolution that occur over various timeframes. From a theoretical standpoint, it is clear that both very short and very long-term periods of time need to be taken into consideration. On one end, rapid changes in population ecology and evolution need to be acknowledged, while on the other end, evolutionary responses to environmental changes need to be aligned with geological timescales. In addition to these disparate timescales, the fact that they often operate independently of each other complicates the picture. In this review, we seek to clarify the various timescales and rates of change involved in eco-evolutionary dynamics, as well as factors that influence and modulate them. In understanding these complex relationships, it is clear that across all timescales and rates of change, the eco-evolutionary dynamics of a system can significantly impact the long-term outcomes and resilience of the system.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can excel in multiple downstream tasks, SUPERB highlights a significant research opportunity. However, SUPERB's design faces limitations, including the small number of evaluated tasks and close connection between pre-training data and downstream tasks, which hinders its effectiveness in identifying resilient speech models. In contrast, an adversary can effectively expose models with poor speech representation by intentionally introducing distortions or manipulations that compromise task accuracy. Inspired by the idea of testing language models with adversarial samples, this research introduces a new adversarial benchmark to assess speech models via the injection of various types of distortions into the training data. This approach evaluates several speech models trained using SUPERB's benchmark with our injected adversarial samples, revealing that model robustness varies depending on the specific distortion and whether the injection occurs during pre-training or fine-tuning. In addition, we investigate the potential of our injected samples as a form of transfer learning to achieve transfer and improve model robustness.

Our research examines how the inherent characteristics of Blockchain-based Decentralized Exchanges (BDEx) affect investor adoption. Unlike centralized exchanges, which ensure security and offer detailed functionality, are limited to specific geographic regions, and subject to stringent regulations, BDExes provide anonymity, broader global access, fewer functional options, and more relaxed regulatory conditions. Using a Bayesian Variable Selection approach, our analysis of BDEx data suggests that security, scalability, and regulatory compliance serve as crucial adoption drivers. This result stands in contrast to the typical investor experience on centralized exchanges. Notably, our findings highlight the distinct preferences of individual investors when choosing between centralised and decentralised platforms.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. This approach is particularly relevant in studies with missing outcomes, where assumptions about data are inherently limited. To address this challenge, the E-value framework is incorporated into a Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis, enabling evaluation scenarios with various types of missing data patterns. However, existing protocols for conducting Bayesian Sensensitivity Analysis are not suitable for situations involving the E-value, due to the inherent subjectivity of assuming missing data values. This article presents a novel protocol for performing Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis for missing data using the E-value, with a primary goal of systematic review investigations. A comprehensive Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis case study is provided, examining a meta-analysis of low and moderate quality studies with missing event data, incorporating different assumptions about data missingness patterns. This research seeks to develop a standardized method for conducting Bayesian Sensitivity Analysis for missing data, leveraging the E-value framework.

This study concludes a comprehensive categorization of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries within the larger framework of the extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}\big]$. Firstly, prior research by the author concerning symmetries involving the Cartan generator(s) with non-trivial actions, and those exhibiting generic behavior, are revisited and verified. A thorough enumeration of non-generic symmetries then follows. These combined categories collectively form an exhaustive compilation of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries in the context of $\mathbb{C}_q\big[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}\big]$.

The emerging concept of Federated Learning addresses the security concerns that arise from personal data sharing due to data breaches. To enhance security, the integration of Blockchain technology into Federated Learning is being explored, particularly to guarantee transparency, integrity, and trust by ensuring that data are reliable and accurately represented. To comprehensively understand the implications and possibilities of combining Blockchain with Federated Learning, a formal framework must be developed. A literature review will examine the effectiveness of combining these technologies and present a comprehensive evaluation of existing approaches, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses. To facilitate an in-depth understanding of this emerging technology, a series of criteria have been developed to analyze the current state of literature. A thorough review of 41 papers is provided, offering critical insights into the feasibility of implementing Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning in the Internet of Vehicles context.

The findings on prompt D meson production agree with theoretical models such as PYTHIA and POWHEG with and without re-summation of hard gluon radiation. The production rates of beauty and charm quarks, in the form of D mesons, are also established with integrated $p_\mathrm{T}$ ranges that differ for mesons with strange quarks (D0, D+ and D*+) and those without (D0 and D+). The produced transverse momentum of these quarks and hadrons are expressed in terms of Lambda. The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in C and Java, 
but a study examining Python crypto APIs has been absent until now. Our investigation 
revealed a substantial number of misuses of Python crypto APIs in real-world projects, 
including some that are widely installed on Linux systems. Our analysis shows that Python 
crypto API misuses can easily lead to security vulnerabilities and code pollution, 
resulting from incorrect or outdated library versions, incorrect usage, and insecure 
password handling. Moreover, the misuses of Python crypto APIs share common causes, such 
as a lack of code review and inadequate documentation, which is compounded by Python's 
characteristics, including its ease and ability to hide errors.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as streetlights. Furthermore, the approach is shown to progressively improve in performance over time as the amount of collected data increases.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms. To achieve synthesize-based sparse deconvolution, we developed the NuSPAN neural network model, combining a convolutional neural network with the proximal average transform. NuSPAN effectively transforms the non-uniform sparse problem into a uniform sparse problem, enabling synthesis-based sparse deconvolution through iteratively reformatting the proxy. Performance tests were conducted using synthetic data from the CMP gather and real-world recordings from the Marmousi2 benchmark and Amazon fan delta, respectively. Compared to established sparse models and deep learning-based seismic inversion techniques, NuSPAN yielded enhanced performance in terms of computational efficiency, accuracy, and seismic image quality.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and has the Veckers type factorizations applied to BMOA_p. We analyze the maximal subgroups, isometries, irreducible elements, semigroups of integral operators within VMOA_p. We also examine the equivalence between the boundedness of A_p and VMOA_p for p >= 2. Furthermore, the article provides an alternative proof for the characterizations of BMOA_p and VMOA_p.

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion and the lengths of operator Deformations. This study introduces a novel, model-independent method for calculating the lengths of operator Deformations by analyzing wavefunction overlaps in a one-dimensional system. It involves computing and subtracting wavefunctions at adjacent sites of ground states in finite-sized systems. This approach was successfully applied to the Haagerup spin chain, allowing for verification of previously conjectured operator Deformation lengths.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistic research, particularly when handling large datasets quickly. Although machine learning models have excelled at POS tagging in modern languages, their performance declines significantly for language varieties that have undergone substantial changes over time. To overcome these challenges, we develop a novel machine learning approach that takes into account the inherent uncertainty present in labeling tasks, especially for language varieties where syntactic patterns have diverged. This innovative method utilizes the set-valued prediction technique, which accommodates uncertainty in labeling by generating a range of possible tags alongside confidence levels. To test its effectiveness, we applied this approach to English and German corpora from the 19th century, examining sets of tags and confidence levels produced. The results indicate that POS tagging with a high degree of accuracy can be achieved for English texts, while also demonstrating promising outcomes for German texts, despite the complexities involved.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a canonical representation for the state of a non-smooth, conservative system. We identify a specific set of geometrical properties that a canonical representation must possess, and establish that such a representation exists uniquely. We further demonstrate that this representation can be constructed by utilizing a particular iteration of the Poincaré-Birkhoff map, which is applied in a manner that differs from the standard approach. We illustrate the theoretical findings by applying them to simple examples, including a smooth pendulum and half pendulum with smooth impulses.

As smart cities expand with infrastructure management systems, they generate an increased need for automated software conversion of human-specified demands into machine-readable formats. This study proposes an intelligent multi-layer interface for accomplishing this conversion by leveraging AI technology to analyze the language and context used in user requests. The system comprises of two main components: the first is a natural language processing module responsible for analyzing the user's needs and creating a formalized representation, and the second is a decision support module that offers a range of solutions for fulfilling the user's request. The system was tested on a dataset from Alborayz Real Estate in Saudi Arabia and yielded a high accuracy rate.

Our research presents a compensation method to rectify errors made by controlled operations in quantum computing. This approach can be applied to correct errors in quantum gates used for quantum information processing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by implementing it in a quantum device produced by Rigetti & Associates and show that it enables the execution of a five-qubit quantum gate with high fidelity using fewer physical gates than would be required with current technology limitations.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism often results in a partial order. However, this property does not hold for the image of a relation under any epimorphism. In the context of regular categories, we investigate the potential to modify the above statements by replacing partial orders with equivalence relations. The stability of the category in question plays a crucial role in determining the outcome, and we establish that the category may fail to have the required property even when it is symmetric and has pullbacks. Nonetheless, if the category has pullbacks, it inevitably has full pullbacks. In regular categories with pullbacks, the image of an equivalence relation often, but not always, results in a partial order, and we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the property to hold universally. The sufficient condition can be interpreted as the pullback preserving character of the category being strengthened.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets captured in different light conditions. To overcome this issue, our approach VT-CLIP uses query refinement through image-text contrasts to enhance the accuracy of visual-class models, where we demonstrate that these refinements can be applied to a range of established models without additional computational costs. Our evaluation across various image-text datasets demonstrates the efficacy of our refinement technique, where we achieve up to a 19% improvement in accuracy based on a range of evaluation metrics. Additionally, our framework facilitates a range of potential applications and can be utilized to address a range of visual classification challenges.

To enhance the efficiency of Krylov solvers for system (2), which may involve random errors, a method called non-uniform Operator Shifting is developed. This method offers a range of options that can be tailored to suit specific non-uniform shifting kernels. This approach can make existing solvers suitable for noisy problems and provides a general framework that can be applied to any method for solving large, noisy matrix systems. Furthermore, a new RKS solver is introduced that can handle both uniform and non-uniform shifting kernels to provide a robust and efficient solution to large, noisy matrix systems. This is demonstrated in a study that compares the performance of RKS and other algorithms in solving a large, noisy hyperbolic eigenvalue problem.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered, and the equivariance group in question is the quaternionic group $Q_8$. In the process, we compute the Mackey functors for $\underline{\pi}_{k\rho} H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate that its tight Hilbert function equals the regular one, thus proving that in this case, the tight Hilbert function is indeed regular. Furthermore, we provide a condition under which the tight Hilbert function of a one-dimensional $F$-local ring has a specific characteristic, thus solving the open problem posed by Matsuda and Nakamura.

The application of machine learning in image assessment is gaining momentum, with the medical imaging community working to establish guidelines for the standardization of image analysis outputs. Through projects like QuIP, the medical imaging community identifies relevant metadata to optimize image analysis, but the current approach relies on customized files without a centralized management system. As a result, the implementation of such metadata is complicated for new projects and tools. To address this issue, the highdicom project was developed. This Python library provides a comprehensive set of tools for encoding machine learning outputs and other relevant data within standard DICOM files. By utilizing highdicom, the process of creating custom annotation files is simplified, allowing for the direct creation of DICOM objects. The library also includes functionality for writing DICOM files and object-level annotations. Highdicom includes pre-built tables for common metadata, such as QuIP and QuIPv2, as well as the ability to incorporate user-defined private data. The library's functionality can be demonstrated through its analysis of lymph node imaging, with the ability to store DICOM data both locally and in cloud-based platforms like Amazon S3. To facilitate widespread adoption, highdicom offers a range of features, including a user-friendly command-line interface, a `to_dict` method for data serialization, and support for multiple file formats. By standardizing image analysis outputs using highdicom, the community can work towards a unified understanding of the data, ultimately enabling tools like registeredML models, model registration, and output

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and demonstrate that the corresponding charge is connected to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, when evaluated on the horizon. The entropy can also be calculated using a Virasoro algebra and Cardy formula approach, in which we identify relevant diffeomorphisms based on a simple physical principle that maintains the horizon structure's invariance. Our method addresses the fundamental, physically meaningful aspect of the holographic principle across the GR-LQG boundary.

In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively applied in dealing with complex genetic data. However, their use is frequently hindered due to a substantial shortage of quality annotated datasets, especially when dealing with tasks related to sequencing data. This issue is addressed by developing novel, unsupervised representation learning strategies grounded in contrastive learning for DNA, ATCG, Nucleotide, and K-mer sequences. According to experimental results, the proposed methods outperform baseline models across the full spectrum of commonly used benchmark evaluation metrics.

Investigating the influence of surface termination on the metal-insulator transitions in thin V$_2$O$_3$ films is crucial for understanding the complex surface chemistry involved. Experimental studies focused on two types of surface terminations, namely oxygen-rich and vacuum-exposed surfaces, utilizing a sequence of deposition and annealing processes. By combining photoemission and x-ray absorption spectroscopies, researchers analyzed the electronic structure of the films. The results revealed a significant difference in the metal-insulator transitions between oxygen-rich and vacuum-exposed surfaces, which could be explained by analyzing the band alignment and density of states. Furthermore, researchers used DFT calculations to determine that the metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ are associated with a semimetal to semiconductor transition and that the vacuum-exposed surface gives rise to a larger semiconducting gap than the oxygen-rich surface. Overall, these findings suggest that the metal-insulator transitions in V$_2$O$_3$ are influenced by the surface termination, and this knowledge can be leveraged to tailor the surface chemistry of other transition-metal oxides through deposition and annealing techniques.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both the general framework and specific steps for this method, considering a moment map that decouples into abelian and non-abelian components. As an illustration of this method's utility, we apply it to a Lie-Poisson equation derived from the N-body problem, demonstrating canonization through a momentum map constructed from the body-fixed angular momentum vector. This method also enables a phase space decomposition that distinguishes abelian and non-abelian parts, allowing for representation of system dynamics within an abelian symplectic space. As shown in the body example, the resulting system dynamics exhibit an additional conservation law corresponding to the decoupling abelian part of the moment map. This method has significant implications for applying geometric mechanics principles to problems previously solved via Lagrangian mechanics, encompassing statistics such as the N-body problem.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of all known microlensing planets discovered through the Sub-Prime Field in the KMTNet Networx survey, which has resulted in the identification of 9 newly identified planets and an expansion of existing knowledge on 5 others. These microlensing planets and their characteristics are detailed in this study. Their mass distribution and orbital periods were found to align with the broader expectations of the Galactic planet population, which suggests a strong case for the planet excess arising from a relatively high ratio of M-dwarf to G-dwarf stars in the surveyed area. It is estimated that roughly 60% of planets with a mass below 0.1 M_J are found orbiting stars with masses below 0.4 M_@. Based on these findings, a hypothesis has been developed which suggests that planets with a mass below 0.1 M_J are predominantly found in systems where the host star has a mass below 0.4 M_@ and the orbital period is less than 5 years. This proposed relationship needs to be verified by future surveys to determine if it is a widespread phenomenon across the galaxy. Key data from the study and relevant figures are detailed below the reference section.

To address a category of optimal control issues for hyperbolic conservation law systems and their regularization versions through viscosity, a comprehensive approach is proposed and implemented. This approach is illustrated through the analysis of the canonical example of the barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Firstly, the necessary condition for entropy - entropy flux - metric in the BNS is identified and implemented. A selected entropy function transforms the BNS into a sum of the metric's flux and the gradient of the entropy. This facilitates the establishment of a metric variational problem, and through this, the first order necessary condition for optimality is derived and implemented. Secondly, a sufficient condition for optimality is identified and implemented within the context of the BNS system. This condition leads to the derivation of an open-loop optimal control method, and is characterized by the dependence of the BNS system solution on the control variable, and to the metric being a convex function of the control variable. Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with widely accepted industry standards, drawing on information like client loan repayment histories and demographic profiles.
This study compares the performance of several machine learning models – Random Forest, Decision tree, KNN, SVM, and XGBoost – using data from a private Ethiopian bank, to determine which model excels on KMeans SMOTE over-sampled data.
Upon conducting the evaluation and exploration of feature selection methods, the results demonstrate that XGBoost achieves the highest F1 score, highlighting that factors such as age, employment duration, and customer account balance hold greater importance than others in predicting non-performing loans.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally discovered by Stanley and later expanded on by Shareshian-Wachs in their $q$-analog, are crucial in their respective contributions to invariant theory and $q$-homology. In particular, the relationships between the CSFs of Dyck paths, the CSF basis, and the principal specializations will be examined, in addition to the relationships between the CSFs of Dyck paths, the CSF ring, and the reduced CSF ring, and the $q$-analog of Ramsey numbers for paths. This will utilize various techniques, including the combinatorial interpretation of Gessel-Viennot and the principles of $q$-rook theory as discovered by Stanley and the second author. These findings are then verified through a comprehensive analysis of the reduced CSF ring of Dyck paths.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), have been found to perform well on various tasks. However, they are not capable of recognizing symmetries in tasks such as orientation recognition in scenes. This limitation is due to DCNNs' inherent assumption of ambient isotropy, which does not accommodate for categorical symmetries. This paper introduces a novel model called the Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCNs), which are based on categorical convolution operators that recognize symmetries in scenes. This is achieved through the use of orientation groups as substitutes for the traditional Euclidean motion group to define convolution operators. The OCNs' architecture is derived from the Sobolev norm-based Categorical Sobolev Spaces (CS Spaces), which are constructed using orientation groups and incorporated into a deep network to enable orientation recognition. Experimental results show that OCNs outperform traditional DCNNs in various orientation recognition tasks.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Subsequently, we examine the spectral outcomes by combining the relative trace formula with the Petersson sum. Ultimately, we translate these findings into a resolution to a problem posed by Waldspurger.

We developed a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses such as the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass for heavy quarks. This method considers the relevance of higher-order quark masses in relation to their expansion in the heavy quark limit within QCD. Specifically, we focused on the pole mass and the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass, as well as the two-loop pole mass, with particular attention to the inclusion of mass effects from heavy quarks with masses slightly above the threshold. Notably, our results show that a minimal set of quark masses up to mass $m_b$ suffices to achieve a high degree of accuracy when computing two-loop pole masses. This finding implies that the choice of the mass value for the heavy quark is largely irrelevant to the final outcome for pole masses at the two-loop level. Moreover, our analysis extends to the one-loop pole mass, revealing that the inclusion of mass effects from lighter quarks such as the ones with masses $m_u$, $m_d$, or $m_s$ is practically undetectable.

Consider a graph $G$ and its subgraph $H$ defined by the subset $V \subseteq V(G)$. The concepts of sequential $k$-edge coloring for $G$ and $H$ are introduced, which respectively utilize $k$ different colors in a specific sequence to assign to each vertex in $G$ and $V$. It's shown that if $G$ has a $d$-edge coloring of sequence type and $|V \cap E(G)| \leq 1$, then $G$ has a $d$-edge coloring of sequence type for $H$. Additionally, certain criteria are established for the application of this theorem. Moreover, the theorem is illustrated with various practical applications including specific graph types such as complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and Möbius graphs.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for 0 < q < 2.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results. Computed Tomography
scans can provide valuable assistance with COVID-19 diagnosis, although they expose
patients to a significant amount of radiation, which can be detrimental to those
receiving repeated scans. To address this issue, we studied low-dose and ultra-low
dose scan protocols, which minimize radiation levels while maintaining image
quality suitable for diagnostic purposes. Since qualified healthcare workers might
be scarce during a pandemic, we designed an artificial intelligence framework to
automatically detect COVID-19 using low-dose and ultra-low dose scans. The model is
based on a two-stage capsule network architecture that incorporates semantic routing
for noise reduction and image enhancement. The framework achieved impressive results,
with 93% accuracy in detecting COVID-19 from low-dose and ultra-low dose scans, 89%
accuracy in identifying pneumonia, and 86% accuracy in identifying acute respiratory
distress syndrome. Furthermore, the framework outperformed several competing models,
including Google's Inception model and the World Health Organization's reference
image database. The implementation details and source code were made publicly
available.

As numerous satellite constellations in Low-Earth Orbit secure funding and plan their deployments in the final stages of their development phases, a pressing issue has arisen regarding how to efficiently manage the space where they operate. To facilitate safe coexistence among these satellites and the services they provide, it is crucial for operators to have an understanding of how to utilize the space they occupy. This paper presents a metric, known as "space occupancy," to measure a satellite constellation's usage of the LEO region. This metric considers a representative spatial footprint each satellite has when passing through a given area in a specific time interval. To determine the occupancy space, we define a 3D tensor field that represents, at each point in the LEO volume, the sum of the distances between this point and every satellite footprint that intersects with it, taking into account the statistical properties of the satellite motion. To test our approach, two cases are evaluated: (i) a satellite moving in a sun-synchronous orbit with a known angular velocity and (ii) a satellite in an orbit with an elliptical shape.
