To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is created initially, which allows for intricate quad configurations. Subsequently, our Integer Linear Programming implementation optimizes the mesh topology, resulting in a high-quality quadrilateral mesh suitable for visualization or further processing. Key features of our approach include its universal applicability to CAD models of any complexity and the ability to produce high-quality meshes with minimal manual input, although fine-tuning may be necessary in complex cases.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently used as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. A limited number of studies have explored the sampling distribution of correlation coefficients. The present research extends existing work by providing precise formulas for the mean, variance, skewness, and k-th moment of sample correlation coefficients. The obtained formulas can be employed to construct approximate distributions of sample correlation, which can in turn be used for conducting statistical tests without relying on asymptotic theory. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to any type of data without requiring specific distributional assumptions, provided that the data points represent independent and identically distributed samples.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

This study focuses on finding a control strategy for the 2D Navier-Stokes equations using a feedback loop in a specific class of Lebesgue spaces. More specifically, it considers the class $L^q$ for $q \in [1,\infty)$ and examines the final strong stabilization of the system in this space using a high-dimensional feedback loop. In doing so, it addresses the issue of stabilization in both Sobolev and Besov spaces that are critical in nature. Furthermore, it makes use of a specific control strategy that localizes the feedback loop spatially and temporally, resulting in a finite-dimensional feedback loop that is implementable. Additionally, it demonstrates the non-uniqueness of weak solutions to the stabilized system under certain conditions.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web browser, that can record and capture word usage videos 
from the internet using mind maps. These mind maps, which serve as dynamic concept 
maps, aim to better represent context-specific word meanings. User studies have 
confirmed that LMD is a useful tool for expansions and user definitions, outperping 
conventional dictionaries. Moreover, the data collected from LMD has enabled the 
generation of context-specific paraphrases for words, as well as the construction 
of a knowledge graph, offering a wealth of data and concepts for NLP models to 
utilize. All data and code associated with this project have been made freely 
available online.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable learning (xAI). This study investigates the accuracy of model-agnostic explanations generated by LIME-RS, specifically in the context of recommendation systems. We focus on two key aspects: the consistency of explanations provided for items with similar attributes and the adherence of explanations to the underlying causality. We modified LIME-RS to generate explanations within a predefined space, using ordinal categorical embedding. Our findings suggest that LIME-RS explanations are consistent, but may not always adhere to causality due to limitations in local LSTMs used to create explanations.

The surface exchange enhancement plays a crucial role in reinforcing electron scattering and thus influences surface and near-surface states within indirect bandgap quantum wells. This research focuses on an InAs/Al$_{0.48}$Ga$_{0.52}$As quantum well grown by molecular beam epitaxy, where an in-situ scannning electron microscope examination revealed a 20 nm thick InAs epilayer. Near-surface state formation in this 20 nm InAs quantum well was found to be 280 meV below the conduction band edge, pinning the Fermi level, where a 6 meV thermal broadening was observed. This pinning was attributed to the surface exchange enhancement, where a comparable thermal surface exchange specie diffusion rate was recorded. Notably, this pinning level significantly diminished to 110 meV below the conduction band edge in a 60 nm thick InAs quantum well, where surface exchange specie diffusion rates were found to be sublinearly proportional to temperature. This study indicates that surface exchange enhancement is the primary mechanism governing near-surface state pinning in indirect bandgap quantum wells, where surface chemistry can be manipulated to produce separate electron and hole gas populations, potentially vital for quantum information processing applications.

Several recent studies have demonstrated that inductively learning concepts from local patterns in data can be remarkably effective. Nonetheless, local information is not always sufficient; numerous examples exist that illustrate conventional features learned from global patterns cannot surpass state-of-the-art performance when modified to accommodate noisy or adversarially manipulated data. Consequently, we investigate the theoretical boundaries within which local learning methods consistently yield reliable results. Notably, our research shows that local learning patterns possess robustness to adversarial tampering in data-massured scenarios, whereas they do not provide much protection against attacks targeting model robustness. Similarly, learning from local patterns is beneficial when targeting model robustness against targeted assaults, whereas it does not provide much protection against unintended assaults. Ultimately, our research uncovers a significant connection between the effectiveness of local learning and data-massured assaults, which highlights the significance of properties like data class balance in determining the reliability of local learning-based algorithms.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This study delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics, identifying and leveraging its diagonalization via a unique set of Householder transformations that utilize a specific, optimal choice of reflection vectors. This results in a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the kernel matrix, accomplished in $O(N)$ time. Furthermore, we propose an innovative solution to the Sinkhorn problem by utilizing the SVD, ultimately leading to an $O(N)$ time solution for the entire iteration. This breakthrough enables the resolution of large-scale ot problems, specifically those involving millions of data points, in a reasonable time frame of seconds to minutes, facilitating novel applications.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an opportunity to link coronal activity with UV fluctuations, particularly in the far-UV range (110-180 nanometers). A study involving Hubble Space Telescope FUV data across multiple occasions revealed AU Mic displays characteristic far-UV fluctuations associated with its coronal activity, but not typically seen in solar flares. During quiescence, AU Mic's FUV spectrum matches PIONIER near-infrared data, but does not match solar or Alpha Centauri A/B spectra, indicating its FUV emission likely originates from a combination of the star's wind and a possible shock near its chromosphere. Flares in September 2019 exhibited FUV jumps similar to those seen in EUV and X-rays, lasting about 2.7 hours, correlating with a possible white-light continuum consistent with a strong flaring corona. Two shorter flares (each about 30 minutes long) were also observed, one matched by a PIONIER light curve, suggesting the FUV and near-infrared flares shared common properties. Analyzing the spectral energy distribution, the study estimates AU Mic's FUV emission is roughly matched by a blackbody with a temperature around 10,000 K,  and the Star-Gravtzeit interaction may be the mechanism

Accelerated charged particles emit electromagnetic radiation as they move through a medium, which in turn can cause them to decelerate. This medium-dependent friction is influenced by factors such as the dielectric constant and magnetic properties. Within a specific range, the dielectric constant impacts the magnitude of the deceleration experienced by the charged particles. This contribution examines the dielectric medium effect on charged particles moving at constant velocities, charged balls, and charged dipole particles. The paper derives relevant equations and provides a comparison with an alternative method.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed by weight adjustment methods which modify how classifiers classify by altering the vote thresholds. Our approach uses a Bayesian framework to develop a novel system of weights centered on the nearest neighbor classifier. This method demonstrates significant benefits, with simulations and real-world data analysis revealing substantially improved accuracy, specifically in cases where data is skewed. Furthermore, the solution can be applied to any nearest neighbor classifier.

The ultra-bright quasars discovered in the Southern Sky by SkyMapper are reported on, with their extensive luminosity range covering seven orders of magnitude. With a record-breaking 68 quasars found at a redshift of z=5, this study challenges previous assumptions and expectations, while also unveiling a group of novel quasars at a redshift of z~6, due in large part to SkyMapper's data. By selecting and analyzing these quasars based on their brightness, a new luminosity distribution is established, with data suggesting that ultra-bright quasars make up around 1 per cent of their overall population. With a complex pattern of variations, this study sets a new model to describe their distribution at different points in time, while also noting that the phenomenon of variability in these quasars is quite extensive, with a significant change observed in their brightness at a redshift of z~5.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable knowledge for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of elusive Majorana modes.

Our research explores the contraction behavior under specific conditions for a particular type of system discontinuities, specifically entropic discontinuities, and includes relevant applications such as shock waves in a particular class of systems known as hyperbolic balance laws, and a broader category of nonlinear conservation laws.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a scene -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that uses a pioneering method for steady view generation. Our approach is founded on conditional diffusion models, successfully produced consistent, plausible views by virtually navigating a scene -- measured by both overlap with the original view and the generated latent code. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with challenging real-world datasets -- CHUBB and LLBB -- by comparing the generated views to those captured by cameras positioned at distinct angles.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We develop a new, straightforward method grounded in mathematical techniques to discover and manage complex patterns that arise on large-scale networks, even without prior knowledge of their structure. This approach identifies underlying dynamics by analyzing a collection of observed data, which it uses to create an optimal control model to predict and manage these patterns. Our proposed method outperforms other techniques in predicting outbreaks on network models, including the basic SIR and network-based SIS models. It also effectively predicts and optimizes using large-scale networks, such as the American Power Grid. Our study demonstrates that this approach can be applied to a broad range of problems in science and engineering. It also provides a valuable tool for detecting and managing complex patterns in many areas of study.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators compared the images taken by both manual and robotic methods. The results showed that robotic scanning produced high levels of reliability, matching or exceeding the reliability of manual scanning in most measures. Notably, robotic scanning exhibited greater consistency than manual scanning in assessing the largest protrusions of the vertebral processes. Furthermore, the combined use of robotic and ultrasound technology enabled some assessments to be more reliable than those obtained through manual scanning alone. The study suggests that robotic scanning can be an effective and reliable tool for assessing scoliosis, and its integration with ultrasound technology may aid in the accurate detection of vertebral protrusions.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to predict median duration values for speech segments. Unlike traditional approaches, this approach doesn't rely on specific probability distributions, reducing the need for subject-matter expertise to adjust model outputs. A median duration can be accurately predicted when sufficient data is available, in contrast to the uncertain estimates provided by prior non-parametric methods. We evaluated the new model and found it to be as efficient as traditional approaches, and the results from subjective evaluations confirm its effectiveness in producing comparable synthetic speech to the original.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent breakthrough in natural language processing tasks such as language modeling, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis has been made possible due to the success of deep learning models. This research introduces a novel deep learning approach for detecting online hate speech using a unique neural network architecture centered on word and phrase features. The model's effectiveness was demonstrated through experiments using four datasets from different languages, showcasing its ability to accurately classify hate speech. A comparative analysis revealed that our approach surpasses existing methods, including models proposed by prior studies.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, a novel MIMO framework is introduced that enables shared feature learning among subnetworks through the use of shared or tied weights. This approach is further augmented by incorporating T5-style relative position encoding to allow subnetworks to learn and process inputs in an ordered manner. Results on standard image datasets demonstrate that this new framework results in significantly improved performance, parameter efficiency, and memory usage while also enhancing the overall interpretability of MIMO networks.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves considering datasets tailored for tasks like document deblurring, layout structure identification, text extraction, and color restoration. A notable pattern in the literature suggests that the majority of datasets for document analysis exclusively cater to modern text-based documents. However, this work focuses on collections of images from older documents, a category sometimes referred to within the broader framework of Document Image Recognition. Our review encompasses the characteristics of individual datasets, including their composition, evaluation criteria, and associated metric values. Notably, this study aims to provide a more complete analysis by accounting for nearly all datasets of this type, unlike existing surveys which often exclude certain collections. Moreover, this work seeks to provide a more authoritative summary by specifying the distinct characteristics of each dataset, in contrast to other studies that may blend or confuse individual datasets within a single description.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving precision in machining tasks using an advanced control algorithm combined with secondary position sensors. This novel algorithm estimates the true position of the lead screw based on information from two sensors and considers the influence of elasticity, inertia, and friction. It achieves this by modeling the dynamic behavior of the actuator and implementing a flatness-based control system. Simulation and real-world testing have demonstrated that this system is an efficient and reliable solution for enhancing precision in transmission systems.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Inspired by the examination of social life patterns, which involve tracking changes in social connections over time, this research proposes the analysis of health trajectories as a multi-faceted approach. This method views the course of a long-term health condition as a dynamic course of events that can be appraised from different aspects. By applying this new approach to understand multiple dimensions of a person's health history, we analyze the effect of early life experiences on later life outcomes using the example of how childhood adversity impacts a person's risk of suffering from a second heart attack. Through an in-depth analysis of this example, we show that early life experiences can affect later life outcomes in different ways and at different stages of a health condition's progression.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping spheres centered on atoms, where charges are calculated using quadrature points. Although the traditional implementation from Becke's original work uses equal sphere volumes, we find this approach to be inefficient and opt for a volume-proportional placement of points instead. We demonstrate that this modification reduces errors significantly, particularly when dealing with smaller basis sets, for electronic energy calculations in relation to the hydrogen atom, SCF models of He, and the water molecule.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the p-SET problem, has been investigated with various limitations applied. Research has shown that when restricted to k-vertex input graphs, p-SET requires at least $O(k^{\frac{5}{3}})$ time, and this bound is tight. When limited by the feedback vertex set size (fvs) parameter, p-SET requires $2^{O(\sqrt{2}) k \log k}$ time, and this is tight for certain graph types. However, p-SET can be solved in $2^k n^{O(1)}$ time with the known fvs limit, and similar results apply to the Steiner Tree problem. When restricted by the clique width (cw) or treewidth (tw) parameters, p-SET requires $2^{\mathrm{O}(k)}$ time and $2^{\mathrm{O}(k)} n^{O(1)} time respectively. Similar research has been applied to the Steiner Tree problem. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, with the given graph having an independent set parameter (indep), requires $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}\;)}$ time, and these results also apply to the Independent Set

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse climates' characterized by high levels of atmospheric water, leading to intense deluges and transport of water mass.  'Hothouse climates' have been found in models and records of past climates, including sections of paleo-ocean records that suggest episodes of significant atmospheric water.  The dynamics of these extreme climate states and the role of precipitation have not been well understood until now, however.  New research using a global climate model has simulated hothouse climates with results including massive daily deluges exceeding 1000 km in diameter, with a correlation between large precipitation events and sea surface temperature.  The ability of the Earth to sustain such large precipitation events has implications for the simulation of past and future climates.  Specifically, while it appears likely that future climates will retain some characteristics of these hothouse climates, they are unlikely to experience the same level of water in the atmosphere as seen in the ancient 'Hoocene' climate of 100 million years ago.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, an expansion of Yang-Mills theory itself. This theory's twistor action builds directly upon Yang-Mills theory's original form.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise, but it relies on the presence of clean labels. However, since manual labeling by experts is time-consuming and costly, it's common for the process to utilize noisy labels obtained from less experienced operators. In this study, a novel method called BLRM has been proposed, which utilizes Bayesian statistics to determine which labels are unreliable. By assuming that noisy labels are randomly distributed among multiple class options, BLRM employs a posterior probability to identify their source. Subsequently, BLRM refurbishes these noisy labels through a process of prediction based on cleaned feature vectors extracted from the given model. Experimental results obtained on two medical datasets indicate that BLRM effectively mitigates label noise, outperforming existing noise reduction techniques. Moreover, the study found that noisy labels of two specific classes were significantly overrepresented on the DXM dataset, while DXM and PDD datasets both contained labels with inconsistent distribution patterns. BLRM's success is attributed to its ability to accurately and consistently refurbish labels.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and any partition of this cube that consists of $m$ sub-cubes. Let's define an interpolation projector that maps vector functions to piecewise-constant functions over the partition. Denote the norm of this projector by $\|P_m\|_B$ and the norm of the interpolation operator it contains as $\|I\|_S$. The ratio of $\|P_m\|_B$ to the norm of the identity operator is bounded above a certain fraction, which depends on the partition and an explicit expression involving the number of sub-cubes, for a broad range of partition schemes that consist of equal-sized sub-cubes.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function. This is exemplified in the cases of regular graphs and semiregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, the CRW is considered in a different graph scenario.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The model by Patel et al. 1984 is a widely used formula that calculates the distance from the wall in turbulent flow given the Reynolds number and a coefficient that can vary between 0.4 and 0.2. This study aimed to establish a link between the coefficient and the attachment points of hairpin vortex structures in turbulent flow. It analyzed data collected from direct numerical simulations using various Reynolds numbers and found correlations between the coefficient and the location as well as angle of these attachment points. This allowed for the development of three new models based on two different methods, one of which involves calculating a coefficient based on the angle of the attachment points or the distance from the attachment points to the point of maximum velocity. These models were then used to compare the performance of the traditional model by Patel et al. 1984 and two alternative models in predicting the effect of Reynolds number on turbulent flow. It analyzed data collected from different turbulent flow simulations and found that the new models perform better than the traditional model in predicting the effect of Reynolds number on turbulent flow.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field dynamics interacting with a non-abelian ferromagnetic magnetostatic field. The effective model represents a combination of three distinct physical systems, namely, magnetized Skyrme model with self-dual solitons, quark-gluon plasma with an external magnetic field, and quantum Hall effect system. The model's configuration space consists of three dimensions, thereby allowing the emergence of solitons possessing topological magnetic charges of ±3. The text further explores the model's magnetic properties as well as its commutative and non-commutative versions derived from the model's coordinate scaling effect.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase diagram under a specific transformation that reverses time and shifts it diagonally in space. Analytically, this system behaves as an array of semimetallic islands separated by islands with Dirac nodes, all occurring in a non-regular pattern. Semimetallic islands have a unique property where their semimetallic nature changes depending on whether time-reversal symmetry is applied once or twice, resulting in a unique symmetry. Furthermore, at low- or high-intensity magnetic fields, the phase diagram simplifies and reveals regular patterns similar to those of a standard Weyl semimetal under a magnetic field with specific flux configurations.

We developed and investigated optical nanoantennas that combine both plasmonic and dielectric properties, specifically, hybrid nanoantennas featuring a U-shaped iron structure integrated with a SiGe quantum dot gain module within a photonic crystal cavity. These nanoantennas were studied using finite element methods and their performance was assessed through their radiative and non-radiative heat dissipation efficiencies. Results showed that the hybrid nanoantennas can achieve high directional light emission efficiency of up to 85% and high brightness limited only by the quantum dot gain module's efficiency. To optimize the U-shape structure, a balance between the magnetic and electric contributions was considered to maximize the x-component of the Poynting vector, thus enhancing directional light emission. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of the quantum dot gain module by replacing it with a homogeneous gain model and optimizing its position within the photonic crystal cavity to achieve enhanced light-emission rates.

Mechanical screening, a widespread phenomenon in granular and solid materials, is rarely encountered in fluids. Its fundamental mechanical principles, however, remain understudied in the context of fluids due to their inherent difficulty in forming and responding to structures. We have observed a unique mechanical effect where a mobile particle creates a screened region around it, filled with power-law-like distributed forces. This effect is more pronounced in granular matter. Utilizing a numerical method and granular experiments, we investigated the dynamics of the screening phenomenon and its interplay with structural responses in materials. A comparative study was conducted between a fluid system and granular matter to validate a theoretical model that describes the characteristic lengths and low-stress regions within the screened area. The numerical and experimental results not only corroborated the theoretical model but also clarified the temporal evolution of the screening phenomenon, revealing a case where mechanical structures in materials can amplify and stretch screening effects.

Utilizing density functional theory, our investigation focuses on the electronic characteristics of silicene, which is capping hexagonal boron nitride with Mn atoms. Mn atoms are positioned at horizontal and diagonal sites on the surface of the boron nitride substrate. The analysis reveals that Mn atoms interact more strongly with the diagonal sites, resulting in a greater magnetic field on adjacent silicene layers. Interestingly, our findings indicate that Mn atoms at diagonal sites lose three electrons, specifically three, while those at horizontal sites lose two electrons, specifically two. The interaction between Mn and boron nitride results in a magnetic influence on adjacent silicene layers. However, our results show that Mn atoms at diagonal sites lose their magnetic properties when in a non-magnetic state of the adjacent silicene layers. Conversely, Mn atoms at horizontal sites retain their magnetic properties, regardless of the adjacent silicene layers being magnetic or non-magnetic.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses an enigma with regards to the distance between its center and the Earth's position along the galaxy's center-axis (R). According to models predicting a supernova explosion occurring very close to the Earth's perspective, the shape description of Sgr A East should exhibit significantly more pronounced effects of R. Conversely, the most established models describing aged shock-precession scenarios suggest a more uniform and rounded appearance for Sgr A East, which, being relatively far from the Earth's perspective, would not exhibit such pronounced effects. Analyzing spectral data from the XMM-Newton satellite, the paper compares the Sgr A East dataset to simulated 2SA054.0-69.4 X-ray data generated through models simulating supernova explosions at various R values, specifically 4, 8, and 12 parsecs. This analysis reveals a marginal fit between Sgr A East data and simulated data corresponding to R equal to around 8 parsecs, suggesting the possibility of a supernova occurring roughly 8 parsecs away from the Earth's perspective in the direction of the galaxy's center-axis (l,s).

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, with a focus on the numerical evaluation of their performance. In this work, we analyze three methods that combine oversampling with class-balanced learning to enhance the performance of machine learning algorithms. The methods were tested on a large dataset of over 47,000 documents, drawing from five distinct sources, with class distributions revealing significant imbalances. The results showed that a straightforward combination of oversampling with class-balanced learning is sufficient to achieve better performance compared to class-balanced learning alone. However, this setup falls short of the performance achieved by a more complex fusion of oversampling with class-balanced learning. Notably, the class-balanced optimizer proved to be the most effective method in this comparison, despite the presence of minority class examples.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID-19 coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 news stories from over 300 outlets between June 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID under 1% across the U.S., less than in the national news. COVID coverage varied significantly with state infection rates, higher in states with lower income and less educated populations, and fewer stories were published in urban areas. Subsequently, our research reveals patterns where local news outlets in states with more COVID cases increased their coverage, but at a slower rate than national averages, and adjustments were made to reflect declining regional infection rates. These COVID coverage trends were also influenced by income level and education, but not urbanization. Furthermore, our analysis shows a positive correlation between news outlet COVID coverage and their audience demographics, particularly in states with lower high school graduation rates. These findings stress the need for future research on the role of local news in informing health policies, especially during crises like the COVID pandemic.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate capabilities for conserving angular momentum, which, when combined with a fast multipole method, enables an O(N) algorithm for resolving SPH's angular momentum conservation issues at large scales. Historically, this O(N) issue stemmed from inaccurate angular momentum computation in SPH, specifically from failing to account for both local and non-local density estimates in the fast multipole type. Our solution combines an adaptive cut scheme with a fast multipole type to address this problem. Our method modifies the fast multipole type by employing a cut off radius at every fast multipole iteration, which, combined with pruning and re-normalization techniques, ensures that our method upholds angular momentum conservation across all scales. Our method achieves this by limiting the fast multipole type's domain to a single particle and utilizes a cut off radius that doesn't exceed one percent of the box size. Our results show that our method successfully conserves angular momentum in both test simulations and three-dimensional rotating disk cases, achieving an accuracy of nearly 100 percent. Our results also reveal that our method's accuracy is largely unaffected by particle rotation velocity, which means that our method's accuracy is not dependent on additional complex parameters. Our method's simplicity, combined with the fact that it doesn't rely on other complex parameters, makes it highly adaptable and expandable.

A straightforward calculation using the Glauber-Mishchenko model demonstrates that the polarization of a proton resulting from the $e \vec {p} \to e \vec {p}$ interaction retains its initial polarization in the longitudinal plane. However, for anisotropic wave functions, the polarization of the proton may also be partially transferred, with polarization of about $5\%$ or less, with the majority coming from the square of the electromagnetic current. The Glauber-Mishchenko approach also reveals the importance of a specific term in the square of the electromagnetic current in determining the amount of polarization transfer in an $Q^2$ range typical of JLab experiments between $1-4\,(\mathrm{GeV}/c^2)^2$. The proposed research plan aims to verify this effect through an experiment where a polarized electron is scattered by a polarized proton and the resulting antiparticle is observed while also manipulating the angle of the scattering relative to the plane of the incident electron. Such an experiment would be carried out at Jefferson Lab's Hall A using a polarized electron beam and a liquid hydrogen target that is rotated to control the plane of the incident electron. The predicted outcome indicates that the polarization of the antiproton will retain its initial plane of polarization.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning algorithms. The approach leverages the behavior exhibited by expert agents when conditioned on specific observation parameters, utilizing this information to generate diverse states that might be challenging for lower-performing imitating agents. Unlike conventional methods, this technique doesn't necessitate access to expert demonstrations beyond the initial trajectory. By focusing on observation parameters, it utilizes fewer steps and memory, thereby improving scalability. During training, the proposed data augmentation is combined with selective curiosity-driven reward attributes to guide the imitating agent's focus on unexplored aspects. Experimental evaluations on diverse environments and setups establish the efficacy of this method for achieving precise expert imitation with reduced samples and memory requirements.

A study of the production of two Higgs bosons in association with a $W$ or $Z$ boson has been carried out using data collected from 2015 and 2016 proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, resulting in approximately 79.2 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy provided by the Large Hadron Collider. The search has considered the branching fractions of Higgs bosons with jets, $\gamma$+$\gamma$, and $\tau$+$\tau$ decays, showing that constraints on Higgs boson pair production cross-section have been set for mass ranges between 140 and 500 GeV, ranging from 0.35 and 0.41 times the standard model prediction, thus excluding new physics that could enhance this process more than expected.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, thereby meeting the necessary phase condition for resonant precession.
Using a compact laser and mass-produced caesium vapour cell, it functions effectively in a 50 microtesla field and has the potential to be applied in portable geophysical magnetic field measurements.
Our results show a Cramer-Rao limited resolution of 50 fT at 1 second sampling rate and a dynamic range of 20 decibels for magnetic field intensity.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a potential dark matter candidate, where the neutralino's long lifespan is attributed to a significant disparity between its B and L lepton numbers. This model also accommodates a heavy Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV and circumvents the chargino neutralino mass gap issue, thereby aligning with the SM particle mass values. The investigation reveals that, at 95% confidence, the decay rate of the dark matter particle should be lower than 0.2 without violating observational limits. Analysis of the FRB phenomenon suggests that, within certain conditions, the dark matter particle can decay up to 0.2 without contravening observational constraints. The analysis of the dark matter particle's decay impact on the Sun's heat conduction also reveals that, in certain cases, the heat conduction brought about by the dark matter particle can reach the range of $10^{-3}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The study exhibits a diverse range of the dark matter particle's properties. The potential of detecting this dark matter particle through the observation of the diffuse gamma ray flux and the energy distribution of the gamma rays from the Galactic Center and Halos is also discussed.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are densely connected. Densely connected networks in this context mean those with a minimum edge count of at least c n, where c is a constant, for n vertices. We've devised two methods for achieving this approximation - the first involves finding a surface topography that closely approximates the minimum with a ratio no greater than (1-o(1))\sqrt{ln n/ln ln n} and is applicable to any dense graph, while the second method builds upon previous work by Lu and Yuan, adapting it for dense graphs while reducing its requirement for minimal edge density. Finally, we demonstrate that an even more efficient PTAS can be applied to any graph if its minimum edge count meets the condition c n for c, for any surface topography of interest.

A stochastic Newton algorithm is proposed for distributed convex optimization tasks. In this algorithm, a consensus mechanism is employed among nodes for gradient and Hessian vector estimates, which are then used to calculate stochastic Newton steps and consolidate via a consensus process. Experimental results demonstrate the anticipated benefits of using Newton methods in terms of faster convergence, which is actually realized even in the noisy environment of practical applications.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as from fine-grained Time Projection Chambers, it may be feasible to identify the direction of recoiling nuclei caused by both electrons and nuclei, given ionization feedback is considered. This study shows that this is indeed the case using simulated experiments with a 1-keV dark matter particle that either interacts via axion-like or axio-electron interactions. Using a standard gas with electron drift and no ionization feedback, we examine the potential for recoil directionality using various metrics. These metrics, indices of dispersion, angular distributions within the plane, and dipolar analysis, can reliably distinguish between the two interaction types when evaluated at different integration bounds, suggesting that lower bounds around 100-200 electrons are sufficient for this purpose.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed an uncertainty-reflective questionnaire format to capture experts' diverse views. Fuzzy set modeling enabled us to incorporate these uncertainties into our analysis. By integrating multidisciplinary expert opinions into our approach, we original research method can provide more equitable and context-aware decision-making in the realm of commercial driving.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in images during testing phase.
In an attempt to address this issue, the challenge employed a diverse set of real-world scenarios: (1) never-seen characters by the model during training phase, and (2) characters seen during training but grouped differently.
To tackle the problem, the challenge proposed a technique that merges character-level recurrent neural network (RNN) models with an attention mechanism for enhancing recognition accuracy.
For evaluation purposes, the challenge utilized a varied dataset consisting of 100 unique characters and two real-world image collections: TALTOY-NLP and FEBSEZEE.
Results showed that the proposed technique achieved an impressive 9% improvement in accuracy compared to traditional OCR methods.
The challenge aims to contribute to the ongoing research in OOV scenarios and plans to expand its scope and influence the trajectory of future research in the field.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables change over time or space, and their analysis involves determining the most likely outcomes in optimization problems. In critical scenarios, finding the optimal solution is difficult, so an improved method would be an efficient approximation. This paper presents a new approximation technique for a specific type of optimization problem in higher-dimensional spaces. It involves geodesic curves in complex dimensional spaces represented by random fields. This technique works by simplifying a complex optimization problem using the properties of these curves. Preliminary results show that the suggested method yields good approximations and its accuracy can be influenced for tailored applications.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.
