In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying gate voltles, facilitated by controlling the Onsager relation. The study showed that spin polarization can be enhanced when energy gaps form in nanoribbons, and this phenomenon is influenced by the width of the nanoribbon and the height of the energy gap. Moreover, spin polarization oscillations can be controlled using gate voltles and ribbon width. The ability to control spin-based transport in these structures makes them suitable for spin-based logic and magnetic switch devices.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and improvements from the work of Bollobas and Tuza along with the continued research of Tuza and others. Later, a closer approximation was found by the work of Nishimura and Wozniak. Our latest findings, in collaboration with the graph theorist Z. Tuza, reveal the exact relationship: there exists a constant c, where the product of the independence number and c values equals the maximum possible value of cycles in the graph, which is later confirmed with further analysis and the use of extremal examples.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. An investigation of the movement of particles at various angles revealed significant anisotropic behavior. It was observed that the trajectory of particles changes depending on the angle of impact, with greater changes occurring at higher speeds, a phenomenon that persists across all three types of collisions. In contrast, the opposite behavior was noticed at lower speeds, with the ruthenium-ruthenium collisions exhibiting the greatest anisotropic effect. Additionally, it was found that the movement of particles changes phase at a specific speed, with the changes occurring more frequently in smaller, faster-moving particles. An model of desktop fluid dynamics was used to predict that the movement of particles should change direction, with the changes occurring more frequently in larger, slower-moving particles. These predictions were found to disagree with the movement of particles created in the largest collisions. An possible explanation for the discrepancy is that the largest collisions create a larger, longer-lasting area characterized by approximate symmetry, with the ruthenium-ruthenium collisions being the first to exhibit this phenomenon.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous scientific and engineering applications. It utilizes a spectral decomposition technique to identify dominant patterns in a time-evolving state space data set, which can subsequently be employed to generate an efficient predictive model. This method has known limitations, however, when dealing with systems featuring high-dimensional state spaces, chaotic behavior, or detailed microphysical considerations. To address these challenges, the method has been enhanced by integrating a sparse-grid technique. This novel combination, referred to as the sparse-grid-based adaptive spectral Koopman method, benefits from the increased computational efficiency offered by sparse-grid techniques. This increased efficiency is particularly significant when dealing with multi-dimensional systems or chaotic behavior, which often involve large, non-local interactions. To evaluate its effectiveness, the proposed method was tested on two complex systems: a globally coupled rossler network displaying chaotic behavior and a solidifying penney using physics-informed machine learning, which simulates the dynamics of a penney dropping through a gravitational field into a melting ice cube.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored, and the reviewed works focus on the utilization of the R-matrix theory and exterior complex scaling approach to study the ionization of atoms and molecules subjected to intense DC electric fields.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes may result in degenerate scenarios where the solution does not exist, research demonstrates that even in such situations, the Sinkhorn algorithm leads to two specific points of convergence. Crucially, these limit points enable the calculation of a solution to a modified Schrödberger problem with a potentially reduced marginal constraint.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated t¯t cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% and amounts to 67.5 pb, which corresponds to 0.9 pb (statistical) ± 2.3 pb (syst. error) ± 1.1 pb (lumi.) ± 0.2 pb (beam). This outcome is consistent with theoretical quantum chromodynamic predictions and offers constraints on the proton's parton distribution functions at large Bjorken-x.

It's logical to assume that the behavior of an attached particle might influence the dynamics of its unattached counterpart in a coupled system. Researchers have extensively studied this relationship in various systems, but a corresponding investigation into the reverse effect remains lacking. This study focuses on the reverse scenario, where the dynamics of an uncoupled particle centrally attached to a coupled system are examined. The study reveals that the overall behavior of the uncoupled particle under centralized constraints is consistently predictable and controlled by a few key dimensionless parameters, which simplifies complex calculations. Interestingly, the study finds that the uncoupled particle's motion can exhibit complete localization in certain conditions. The study presents a general theory applicable to different types of central coupling and confirms its validity through comparisons with existing literature on anharmonic potentials as well as Monte Carlo simulations. The study's findings on localization in particular and the general theory in general can benefit the ongoing research in quantum dynamics as a practical aid.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}^2-1)$, $(1/c)({u}_{p,b,c}-1)$, and $(1/c)({u}_{p,b,c}-z)$ 
to meet the requirement $(1+Az)/(1+Bz) \prec {u}_{p,b,c}(z)$, allowing for the derivation of sufficient 
conditions for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be in the Janowski class. Specific protocols are provided to create 
univalent functions of the form ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized user IDs spanning 25 months, including pre-pandemic and pandemic periods. It reveals a substantial decline (by 15% to 55% reduction) in urban diversity, with specific activities (such as dining, shopping) experiencing the steepest drops. Notably, individual choices during the pandemic led to a more uneven mix of urban encounters, later exacerbated by increased socioeconomic disparities following non-binding government orders. Our research indicates that reversing these changes will necessitate a combination of collective effort and purposeful intervention to revive urban diversity.

This research project focuses on the development of nonlinear field-split preconditioners for solving two-phase flow problems in heterogeneous porous media, with a primary interest in their ability to achieve efficient computation times on high-performance computing platforms. Two novel preconditioners, the nonlinear multupling of the mass matrix Newton method and the nonlinear control theory Slaving method, were investigated and carefully compared to a widely established standard, the linear two-phase flow Slaving method, using a range of test cases and performance evaluation tools. The study's findings indicate that the nonlinear approaches demonstrate better computational performance and reduced memory requirements, while the linear Slaving method exhibits greater robustness in challenging computational conditions. The discovered patterns and insights from this research can potentially be extended to the solution of more complex flow and transport problems, promoting advancements in efficient simulation methods.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in nature, including predominantly left-handed individuals. Chiral optical cavities can produce unique light emissions with specific polarization characteristics. However, the majority of chiral optical cavities exhibit both a chiral structure and a balanced chirality, resulting in emissions with polarizations that can be either entirely left-handed or right-handed. To achieve a broader understanding and application of chirality, it is often necessary to configure the cavity so that it naturally favors and enhances left-handed or right-handed properties while minimizing or eliminating right-handed or left-handed properties.

The paper presents a novel approach for designing chiral optical cavities using two identical chirally asymmetric mirrors and an unchirally symmetric cavity gap. The results demonstrate that in the single-handedness chiral optical cavities, only left-handed or right-handed electromagnetic waves can resonate within the cavity. Additionally, the paper discusses the properties of p and s polarizations in relation to chirally asymmetric mirrors and establishes a method for calculating the resonance frequency shift. It has been observed that the cavity gap width has a greater influence on resonance frequency shift than the gap width in conventional chiral optical cavities. The proposed single-handedness chiral optical cavities have the potential for various innovative applications in natural phenomena investigation, ChGAP-based research, and optical spintorque mediation.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary terms, extends to annulus amplitudes. Notably, the boundary term related to the Liouville CFT fails to pose the non-rationality problem that would normally make calculation of the annulus amplitude ambiguous. Furthermore, the paper discusses two distinct methods of determining the boundary free energy of the JT gravity model with a single saddle-point and a random distribution of poles inside the annulus.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric has the speed of light as a minimum limit. This is because the warp drive doesn't move but instead warps space-time around it. However, developing the theory further requires finding a solution that can describe the warp drive externally, which has proven difficult. To overcome this, we use the Darrow metric, combined with two perfect fluid equations that include a perfect fluid and a cosmological constant, to find a new set of spacetime solutions. These solutions, known as perfect fluid warp drive solutions, have a newly discovered metric that allows us to separate the spacetime into different components based on the Kretschmann scalar analysis. This gives us two new geometries representing isolated and multiply isolated spacetimes. These findings provide a new framework to explore the geometry of the warp drive spacetime, which can be admissible even without the cosmological constant.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these issues, a fully functional underground infrastructure data management platform is needed, supporting both system assessment and city planning. To address this need, a comprehensive framework for managing underground infrastructure systems as a unified entity has been developed. This framework incorporates citywide, digitized infrastructure data along with geographical information and related properties. A demonstration platform, called GUIDES, has been implemented to showcase its potential applications, including real-time underground mapping, feature extraction using AI and GIS, and spatially-aware data management.

To study the behavior of ultracold ions, it is essential to analyze both the motional states of the ions and the environment. This is particularly crucial for 2D ion crystals where the reduction of excitations and environmental interactions with the surrounding modes needs to be investigated further. This work involves the examination of a 32Magnesium ion crystal trapped using a far-DC electric field, where the breathing mode and center-of-mass mode exhibit distinct spin dephasing behaviors due to differences in mode temperatures. Additionally, the study utilizes numerical simulations, which reveal that the rate of mode temperature increase is primarily driven by the specific driving methods employed. Notably, the study concludes that using a linear motional state distribution is more effective in suppressing spin dephasing in comparison to traditional approaches.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. It relies on extremely close probes that interact with the surface molecules, whose exact influence on the measurement outcome remains unclear. A new approach models the probe as a tiny quantum dot and computes its effects on a molecular target using first-order perturbation theory based on the Dirac equation. The method calculates a modifying factor for each atomic orbital probability in the presence of the probe and considers this within a time-dependent Schrödinger equation framework to determine electron probability densities. These probability densities are then used to determine electromagnetic and chemical interactions between the probe and the surface. The method has been successfully tested on hydrogen and water molecules and compared to experimental data, showing a good match. An analysis of the results reveals a connection between the probe's electron density and the primary target area for different chemical and electromagnetic TERS signals.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and total intensity images at 18.5 GHz, and average intensity maps at 18.5 and 24.5 GHz, we searched for excess emission beyond the expected thermal and synchrotron components. Non-detection in the three sauces of excess emission was found for the observed galaxies' fields. An upper limit on the AME surface brightness of about 0.04 Jy/arcmin^2 (3 sigma) was set at frequencies between 18.5 and 24.5 GHz. It has been observed that AME is possibly not ubiquitous and its occurrence may be limited to certain environments. Diffuse emission beyond what's expected from thermal and synchrotron components was detected for M 31 but it was found not to relate to AME. Also its position and intensity do not match those observed by Herschel. Any radio emission observed at 8 GHz from M 31 up to its central part can only be attributed to thermal and synchrotron components.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For centuries, the origin of these properties has been a topic of debate; two contrasting theories, one involving a straightforward union of ammonium and sulfate ions and the other involving a shared hydrogen bond network, have been proposed. Our investigations using neutron scattering and computational modeling, however, suggest that the two ammonium ions in the unit cell interact with different intensities, with one bond being stronger and the other weaker, pointing to the entropic costs of converting between these states as the source of the entropy change and thus explaining the Union-Crystal-Union phase transition sequence.

In probabilistic learning, organisms often adjust their responses based on unexpected outcomes, referred to as prediction errors. This mechanism is particularly effective when outcomes are unpredictable. However, when outcomes are consistent, naive systems typically favor low-level noise over trying to learn. This scenario is referred to as the exploration-exploitation balance and is crucial for adaptive learning. A recent study discovered that people sometimes employ a suboptimal strategy, characterized by a low-level noise-like approach, when learning from unpredictable sequences. This strategy was also linked to an overestimation of unexpected outcomes, an issue known as an absolute bias. Notably, this study found that individuals who demonstrated a strong bias towards low-level noise-like strategies showed a more pronounced activity in the brain regions associated with reward assessment while learning from unpredictable sequences. This suggests a common underlying brain mechanism may favor adaptive strategies over absolute biases.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems, to investigate quantum contextuality and entanglement. However, another setup using 120 states is needed to fully explore these phenomena.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure capable of efficiently identifying closest shape approximations within a predefined metric, where all approximations lie within a certain distance from a given query shape, with the distance between the query shape and any member of the set being c times the original distance. A prior study showed that solving the Frechet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem for a set of m d-dimensional points using a certain data structure would take at least O(d^2 log^2m) or Ω(d^3) depending on the dimension, with results varying based on construction methods. A more recent study improved these results, narrowing the gap for high-dimensional and low-dimensional search space, including one-dimensional time series. A new approach, based on Ramsey theory, yields more efficient results for certain time series approximations. For one-dimensional time series, the study provides multiple variants of bounds, with significantly improved results, including one variant yielding a linear failure rate, and an inner approach matching this result, offering significantly tighter bounds than previous estimates. A new approach, based on Ramsey theory, yields more efficient results for certain time series approximations, including a new inner bound matching an inner bound of a previous estimate. A different method, Ramsey tree folding, provides even tighter bounds, and analysis of its limitations reveals that this result is near the best achievable, with results varying based on dimension, with low-dimensional results varying based on the number of dimensions

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is that they discard data points affected by measurement error. Our iterative Bayesian unfolding algorithm addresses this shortcoming by using all available data to derive a more accurate error model, thus enabling reliable parameter estimation even with increased noise levels. Our development focuses on estimating physical parameters in experiments with multiple outcomes, such as quantum entanglement formation. Our initial results, obtained through simulations with real data from a quantum simulator, demonstrate that our approach can reliably determine parameters with high precision, up to a certain level of noise. Our analysis reveals that our method's performance depends on the number of outcome channels and the level of coupling between different processes, which influences its reliability.

When humans operate robot arms, it's often assumed that the goal is to execute a specific task. However, when using a robot for tasks like picking up objects, it's more beneficial to establish clear working practices. Our research focuses on an approach where both the operator and the robot contribute to defining these procedures. We allow users to express their preferences through unimpeded interactions, and the robot responds by adapting its behavior to optimize effectiveness and clarity. As the robot refines its tactics, it selects the actions and sequences that result in the best outcomes while ensuring effortless communication. We introduce a method for evaluating the operator's expectations and document the results of a user study with this shared control approach.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, an effective mapping system that automatically adapts to new environments' dimensions and topologies is necessary. Current mapping approaches, such as SLAM, may struggle to navigate areas with large spatial or directional complexity. To overcome these limitations, a proposed unified robot mapping framework incorporates a hierarchical structure that dynamically adjusts its topology in real time based on the size of the environment, using an algorithm that detects topological changes in the robot's trajectory. This robot mapping framework is capable of navigating unfamiliar environments of any scale by maintaining accurate metric and topological relations between locations, thus facilitating navigation and metric calculations within these areas.

Research focuses on multivariable functions to construct inter-group complementary code sets and two-dimensional Z-complementary array code sets, specifically addressing sequences. Eleven main categories of multivariable functions are analyzed, enabling the construction of sequences from two different domains - space and time - to various dimensional spaces. The paper explores general construction methods using functions from different domains and specific examples are provided to illustrate various possible sequences. These constructions lead to general and specific sequence code sets, including those for 1-D and 2-D arrays, to multiple dimensional spaces. Examples illustrate that the proposed sequences achieve optimal or near-optimal Northcott numbers, demonstrating their efficiency.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both raw data and image-based applications. Although it provides an overall comprehension of the body's structure, its reliability can be compromised due to various external factors such as radiation, equipment, and data processing errors. As a result, image distortion, data corruption, and inaccurate material composition measurements occur. To address these issues, a multi-faceted approach is developed by reformulating a previously introduced model that originally dealt with polyenergetic image reconstruction, noise reduction, and material analysis. This enhanced model now includes terms that account for the diversity of x-ray energies, image quality enhancement, and multi-component image decomposition. Inspired by the properties of anisotropic diffusion and its ability to handle disparate signal sizes, a new method is proposed to handle image denoising and material decomposition simultaneously. Although initially introduced as a technique for polyenergetic image reconstruction, its potential is leveraged to solve a more complex problem. By combining various image analysis techniques into a single model, image quality, information richness, and accuracy are simultaneously improved. To validate this approach, comprehensive numerical simulations are conducted, followed by a comparison with established techniques.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates an unrealistic, damped transition. Notably, the described phenomenon aligns with observations of light interaction with coupled metallic particles recorded in recent research studies.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-dependent term relevance, (2) that extracting context-specific information with relevance guidance is more effective than without it, and (3) that human-provided feedback can be automated – namely, that users' selections of relevant terms can inform future query expansions. This discovery prompts us to develop a Expectation-Maximization algorithm that utilizes users' initial relevance labels to identify both context-dependent terms and their corresponding labels, ultimately resulting in a substantial improvement in performance from 51.6% to 67.4% precision at top-1 when compared across 15 queries sourced from Reference Extraction workbench.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When analyzing this type of data, the focus lies in understanding variations that occur both within and beyond time intervals, as well as across different entities when multiple subjects are involved. In contrast, the study of longitudinal data, which tracks changes in individuals over time, differs from analyzing data that spans a broad and uniform distribution of means. To effectively analyze both types of data sets, the goal lies in identifying patterns and variations that occur both chronologically and statistically significant. However, current data visualization techniques often fail to accommodate both forms of analysis, forcing users to decide between them. Therefore, to facilitate interactive data analysis, the developers propose a time-based data visualization approach that allows for both longitudinal and comprehensive analysis. By leveraging this approach, users can explore data at both individual and collective levels, thereby understanding both spatial and temporal patterns. To achieve this goal, the developers utilize an algorithm that identifies patterns similar to a "flat cluster" arrangement, which helps in exploring data set components. In addition, the developers create an algorithmic rule that aids in analyzing both longitudinal and comprehensive data sets. Both algorithms can be used in conjunction when analyzing both types of data sets. To validate its effectiveness, the developers implemented both algorithms using JavaScript and AJAX, thereby incorporating them into a comprehensive data analysis tool named TimePlay. TimePlay incorporates data display capabilities rooted in time, which comprises a plot display

The promising effect of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has garnered significant interest from both academia and industry. Due to the diverse nature of EHR data, incorporating multiple types of clinical information is crucial for identifying similar patients. However, patients with similar properties but different types of clinical information may not be considered similar. Existing patient similarity metrics fail to accommodate this aspect of heterogeneity, thus limiting their capabilities to identify similar patients. This paper presents a novel approach that addresses the issue by proposing a graph neural network model that integrates and merges clinical information from multiple sources. By doing so, this method can effectively detect patient similarities beyond the limitations of the existing methods. Experimental results validate the superiority of the proposed method, demonstrating its ability to accurately identify similar patients with better precision and recall rates.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a soft material. From the free energy model derived from Poisson-Boltzmann, the electrostatic potential and ion density are determined. The boundary of the soft material is represented by a specific type of charge distribution. The results show how the electrostatic potential and ion density change with the soft material boundary's characteristics, such as the distribution of charges and the flexibility parameter, in addition to solvent effects. These modifications cause the electrostatic potential and ion density to decrease near the soft material boundary and the region known as the electrostatic shielding length. This study provides a foundation for understanding the characteristics of the electric double layer at the boundary of a soft material.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like FastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal Request For Information (RFI) documents. The fine-tuned BERT model achieved encouraging results on the PURE dataset, demonstrating superior performance on binary sentence classification with a high level of precision and recall while remaining adaptable to varied writing styles and requirement representations in real-world scenarios.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a large number of relays. To maximize energy efficiency, we develop an optimization problem involving multiple variables that account for the transmission rates of users, the power allocation among users and relays, and the assignment of active and inactive relays. To solve this complex optimization problem, we first simplify its structure by utilizing the duality and convexity of specific components. We then formulate a series of linearly-constrained optimization problems that jointly determine the power allocation among users and relays, and the assignment of active and inactive relays. Finally, we establish that the global optimality is achieved and present a simple iterative algorithm to solve these optimization problems, which outperforms traditional methods by up to 100% in terms of energy efficiency gain. Simulation results confirm that our proposed scheme leads to significant energy savings compared to traditional methods, especially when the number of relays is large.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model takes into account the unique properties of the host material, including the influence of superconductivity, and can be applied to systems featuring multiple magnetic impurities. It provides an expression for the combined spectral density of spin-resolved low-temperature photoemission spectra. An in-depth examination of the underlying physics has been conducted, focusing on the relevant excitations and approximations applicable to a specific system involving manganese impurities on the Nb(110) surface. Calculations using the established model demonstrated satisfactory agreement with available experimental data. Adjustments to specific parameters were implemented in order to better fit particular results, showcasing the predictive capabilities of this theoretical approach. An analysis of the parameters influencing spectral features revealed various relevant energy scales within the system. Additionally, modifications to the model's approximation scheme were explored, given that excitations beyond the approximate threshold begin to contribute significantly to spectral properties below 10 meV.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has announced the initial investigation into the $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$ decay via a new approach called "decay-in-flight". This research utilized a proton beam targeting a fixed target producing $K^+$ mesons, which were detected, tracked, and identified at the CERN North Area. Following the analysis of a 2018 data set, one candidate event was discovered, which corresponds to a branching ratio estimation of a fraction of a ten-thousandth, in agreement with the Standard Model predictions.

Recent advancements in LiDAR-based mapping technologies have led to increased demand for highly accurate point cloud mapping, particularly in self-driving cars and virtual sensing applications. The main constraint here is real-time performance, prompting researchers to explore deep learning approaches to solve this problem. The key challenge in deep learning-based mapping involves reducing bias in point cloud mapping to achieve more accurate results. This study proposes a novel method, the DNN filter, to address this issue in deep learning-based mapping. The proposed method combines a biased mapping surface and a fine-detail adjustment layer to minimize bias, resulting in a low-latency mapping surface. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed DNN filter by integrating it with a recent deep learning-based mapping scheme, showing a significant 90.6% improvement in mapping accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method is shown to handle dynamic scenes, such as moving vehicles and pedestrians, to enhance safety.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and large volumes of annotated data. The 
lability of these models in unpredictable environments and high data costs have 
hindered their practical application. This research aims to bridge this gap by 
proposing a data-driven, shallow edge detection model that leverages local 
image features and is robust in resource-constrained settings. By utilizing a 
combination of orientation-sensitive Gabor filters and a weighted edge 
detection operator, this model effectively identifies edges within images. The 
model's simplicity and efficiency result in substantial cost savings and superior 
performance compared to deeper, more computationally intensive deep learning 
based alternatives.

We present a detailed model explaining the dynamic process of electronic transitions during X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy, focusing on outer shell absorptions at high fluences. This model reveals that outer electronic states undergo rapid changes due to excitations, decays, and relaxations. Initially, outer outer-shell electrons remain relatively unchanged until outer-shell excitations prompt a cascade of autoionized transitions, leading to inner-shell excitations. This autoionized state then decays through a competitive balance between recombination and further autoionization. While this inner autoionized state can decay through Auger transitions, its inner shell autoions can directly participate in outer outer-shell excitations, initiating a complex multiple-excitations scenario. This work identifies the various electronic configurations possible for outer shell absorptions at high fluences, highlighting some key features observable in XANES experiments - most notably, a resonance peak around the threshold, a prominent feature around $s^0$-resonance, a shoulder around $s^1$-resonance, a peak around $\sim 10$ eV below the threshold, and another around $\sim 20$ eV below the threshold. This model predicts local maxima/minima around resonance peaks and specific energy shifts relative to threshold.

In the context of machine learning applied to communication systems, a widely adopted generative adversarial network (GAN) approach has the effect of stabilizing the system's feature extraction. Consequently, the task of classification becomes simplified. Nevertheless, the learned features are susceptible to disruptions from adversarial attacks, which can have a profound impact on the system's performance. This drawback is addressed by employing a novel mixture GAN approach that incorporates noise augmentation and results in the learning of more robust features. The empirical evaluations, conducted using the BPSK, QPSK, and 8PSK modulation schemes, demonstrate that the proposed approach leads to enhanced resistance against adversarial attacks. The complexity of the GAN model was found to have a limited influence on the attack resistance, while the use of noise augmentation was identified as the primary factor contributing to improved performance. The proposed approach was also observed to outperform traditional adversarial training in terms of classification performance.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts still struggle with.
Researchers have created a notable impact with deep learning-based segmentation, but the task is far from over. Most studies have relied on a single, centrally collected dataset of annotated images. This issue may contribute to issues of low resource availability in the field. We have assembled a unique dataset with 106 datasets from 25 hospitals, totaling 85,392 lesions and 8,053 volumes. This dataset is known as the multi-hospital dataset. We have conducted a series of experiments, including direct comparisons, sequential training, and self-supervised approaches, to identify which method is most effective. Interestingly, the results show that sequential training outperforms direct comparisons and self-supervised methods when working with different datasets. The multi-hospital dataset is and will be publicly available at https://doi.org/10.34770/8g8g6v2.

A type of comparison between comparing functors was introduced by Baratin and Alain in 2018, specifically focusing on $2$-functors that map categories to categories, and has since been further explored by Sheng in studying $n$-functors that map categories to categories for all $n \geq 2$. This paper contributes by defining and understanding bipolar comparison between comparing functors of different types, specifically between $(n+1)$-functors and $n$-functors that map categories to categories for $n \geq 2$. A key type of bipolar comparison, specifically weakly initial bipolar comparison, is established and a critical characterisation of these functors is obtained based on the existence of weak initial stacks for categories. Another type of bipolar comparison, specifically initial bipolar comparison, is also obtained under certain conditions involving full subcategories of pseudofunctors. The study further reveals relationships between different types of equivalence relations, specifically the category equivalence, quasi-equivalence, and $\infty$-equivalence, and demonstrates that these can occur simultaneously in certain cases. A proof that the 2-functor category is preserved under bipolar comparison is also provided.

Our proposed method captures a dynamic system's model error using a recursive neural network (RNP), allowing it to be applied broadly across different types of data. Initially, we provide theoretical justification for the concept of model error in an exact map, which we later generalize for approximate maps. For instances where detailed data is missing, we present an empirical approach to define model error based on the dynamics. In cases involving time series data from an exact map, we develop a framework that identifies the dynamic RNP that matches the model error. Furthermore, we provide a strategy to find the dynamic RNP even when the model error map is unknown, based on approximating the surrounding dynamics. Extending this idea to four example systems demonstrates its efficacy in locating the dynamic RNP, even in cases involving non-trivial error patterns.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals a high mass function, peaking around 10 solar masses with some cores reaching up to 30 solar masses. By matching extinctions to core properties, it's found that most of these massive cores lie along a specific filament. With temperatures around 17 Kelvin and total projected extinction ranging from 2 to 5 magnitudes, they meet the requirements for forming high-mass stars. Therefore, it's concluded that these massive cores are in the initial stages of forming high-mass stars. Furthermore, it's observed that both massive and lower-mass cores have a similar distribution of accretion rates, suggesting that high rates contribute to the growth of these cores. As a result, it's likely that most of the cores in the Dragon cloud have the potential to become high-mass stars, meaning that there could be a significant number of high-mass stars forming across similar clouds.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe following the "big bang" are proposed to be the cause of a significant portion of the universe's total dark matter. To study these black holes and their potential role in creating the dark matter, a new population synthesis tool called PopSyCLE has been developed. In this research, we examine the use of PopSyCLE to analyze a specific PBH model where the formation of these black holes creates the dark matter and find that this model fits data on the relationship between two universal laws of energy and density quite well, although it does not fully explain a specific anomaly in this relationship. Additionally, we find that this PBH model creates a set of universal density fluctuations.

We examined systems of hard wedges, formed by three-dimensional balls, with
the upper two wedges having their bases touching, at various compression levels,
from discrete to continuous particle simulations, for an extensive range of wedge
angles (from 0 to π). Phase patterns were consistently found across different
simulation approaches and confirmed through density profiles and radial distribution
function analysis. These systems exhibited phase transitions, including two-fold
and multi-fold crystallization, influenced by the wedge angle; splay modulation,
with specific wave vectors, also arose in these systems; and coexisting phases
were observed over specific compression ranges. Notably, the splay modulation in
these systems led to two-fold crystallization, appearing at lower compression
levels and broader wave vectors, implying its contribution to this phase.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for handling multiple tasks, and underlines the crucial importance of special tokens in pre-trained language models.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preferences instead. The approach proposed in this work relies on Recurrent Neural Networks to create a context-sensitive system for ranking preferences. The efficacy of this model is tested using real-world data related to software requirements and compared with a context-insensitive baseline. Furthermore, we examine the limitations of our context-based method due to its reliance on a black-box preference system, which hinders its interpretability.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interlinked according to the fundamental thermodynamic relations of Euler's homogeneity theorem. This discovery leads to a generalized expression for the total entropy as the sum of configurational and energetic entropy. This total entropy is linked to the total system energy by a parameter-based expression analogous to the Euler homogeneous function. This finding enables the separation of the total system entropy into two distinct components at any given temperature. Our analysis shows that the energetic entropy component decreases as the total system energy increases. This leads to the phenomenon of dynamic entropy reduction, where the energetic component's decrease causes the configurational entropy reduction, resulting in dynamic density of states reduction and corresponding low-temperature energetic barriers. This phenomenon is the primary cause of the thermodynamic and dynamic hump, supporting the two-step relaxation hypothesis in glass theory.

This study examines how contemporary language models cope with negation in sentences, particularly in contexts where negation interacts with temporal expressions, as researched in developmental psychology. We focus on the interactions between negation and age-related information, and the model's ability to incorporate negation cues and time-related details. Unlike previous analyses that only considered the presence or absence of negation, this investigation explores the type and scope of negation in temporal expressions, and its impact on age-related information. Unlike prior studies that only looked at the presence or absence of negation, this research explores the type and scope of negation in temporal expressions, and how it affects age-related information. The findings indicate that size-based models, such as BERT and BART, can identify negation in temporal expressions, but struggle to accurately incorporate this information with age-related information. In contrast, transformer models like RoBERTa and XLNet demonstrate a better understanding of negation in temporal expressions, especially when combined with age-related information.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from symplectic Poisson structures through connections and curvatures, highlighting how these weights can be viewed as derivatives of symplectic structures on higher-dimensional polytopes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these curvatures weights ultimately reduce to a specific type of Weil algebra when the underlying Poisson structure is nilpotent and free.

This study involves three large-N gauge theories with adjoint fields that have a large number of fields, $N$, where an imaginary chemical potential is introduced. When calculated, the thermal entropy is found to be equal to the entanglement entropy of the center slice across the center of a spatial slice. A large-N formula for the number of degrees of freedom is derived analytically through the use of large-N expansions and Witten index calculations. This theory is then compared to a 4D ${\cal N}=1$ superconformal theory with a specific gauge group and adjoint field that has U(1) symmetry properties. An additional relationship between the number of degrees of freedom and coupling strength properties is discovered within this superconformal theory, showing an AdS/CFT equivalence with a specific 5D warped AdS spacetime. This relationship generalizes to any value of the coupling, including strong-coupling behavior. This was accomplished by solving Witten-Salomon equations for a specific large-N limit using a method of differential equations.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies their framework to a broad class of models that use compound Poisson-type models based on random variables. It provides alternative methods for pricing two types of Asian options, namely, geometric and jump. The analysis offers closed-form solutions for the prices in a manner consistent with Cai, Song and Kou's work. The main advantage of this approach lies in its ability to use a single method for calculating prices, which can then be approximated numerically using a single method.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. Researchers conducted a study that simulated the gamma-ray emissions from cosmic clusters, using data from 79 clusters to create a model. Their analysis suggests that cosmic clusters could account for up to 100 percent of the diffuse gamma-ray background, particularly in the higher energy gamma-ray spectrum. Furthermore, this finding could have a significant impact on existing cosmological models, and may eventually preclude the need for new theoretical models to explain these phenomena.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can manifest as gravitational waves, which may lead to an observable signal in the universe's early stages. In this study, we investigate the potential for these features to cause cosmological collider phenomena within the universe's early periods. A specific example considered is the generation of heavy particles with spin, which produce a characteristic pattern in the gravitational waves known as "harmonics." The appearance of these harmonics in the gravitational spectrum is associated with periodic peaks caused by the movement of particles back and forth through the sound speed. These harmonics can serve as a distinct sign of particle mass and sound speed, as well as any peculiarities or features in the primordial scalar field. Furthermore, the study finds that if certain conditions are met - specifically, if scalar waves from primordial features or other sources are not overwhelming and if gravitational waves from particles with spin are relatively young compared to the time scale of changes in the universe's expansion - then the features caused by the movement of heavy particles with spin (or similar phenomena) can lead to a significant and lasting impact on the gravitational wave spectrum.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. The problem with many existing methods is that they rely on simplifications such as the need for a fixed number of explanations or assumptions of linearity. In response, researchers have proposed the filter attention approach, leveraging the structure of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to overcome these limitations. The model uses a novel loss function and training regimen to highlight the most important image regions for classification tasks, and a subsequent evaluation showed that these explanations align with human expectations. The proposed LSFA approach outperforms existing methods in several evaluation metrics and tasks, including image recognition and explanation.

Research suggests that superconductivity in high-Tc cuprates may be influenced by electron-phonon interaction. To explore this hypothesis in one-dimensional (1D) cuprates, a model was established incorporating the dimerized 1D Mott insulator with electron-phonon coupling. Results show that in 1D cuprates, phonon-assisted electron-electron attraction can function over significant temperature ranges. Moreover, it has been discovered that in 1D cuprates containing polar phonons, a long-range attractive potential arises at high temperatures due to the acoustic phonon assistance. Additionally, it has been observed that in 1D cuprates containing non-polar phonons, an attractive potential arises only at very low temperatures. Moreover, a long-range attractive potential also arises from polar phonon assistance at low temperatures. Moreover, it has been found that in 1D cuprates containing polar phonons, an attractive potential arises only at low temperatures when the phonon displacement is constricted, or in the presence of a bath of classical phonons when the phonon displacement is not constricted. Moreover, it has been observed that in 1D cuprates containing non-polar phonons, an attractive potential arises only at low temperatures when the phonon displacement is constricted, or in the presence of a bath of classical phonons when the phonon displacement is not constricted. The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the factors driving the epidemic. This study proposes a novel causal learning approach to identify key drivers from the Mini Cohort dataset, which is drawn from the Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project. This method involves leveraging both causal structural learning and conventional feature selection techniques for comparison. The results of this study demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and highlight its potential to inform HIV epidemic research.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, we observe a complete transition from a skyrmion lattice formed through nucleation to a homogenous magnetization state, without going through any phase transitions, at a specific temperature. The transition is confirmed through X-ray diffraction and shows clear signs of the breakdown of topological charge as the temperature approaches its critical point. The critical temperature exhibits thermodynamic stability as it persists after multiple heating and cooling cycles. Our findings indicate the formation of stable skyrmions within a chiral magnet, offering insights into the development of novel technologies that utilize topological effects in magnetic fields.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations and visual explanations, focusing on 
particular topics such as model estimation and its underlying techniques, 
initial outcomes and derivations, and applicable uses and implications. The 
model in high-dimensional time series analysis is closely examined, emphasizing 
key assumptions and their roles. The model's capabilities and limitations are 
also critically evaluated. Priorities for future research are suggested at the 
conclusion.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems such as variational inequalities, optimization problems, and different types of operator equations as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist in characterizing the predictive model's uncertainty, which is detrimental for steganographic detection and capacity, ultimately affecting the overall steganography performance. To address this concern, we present a solution by adopting the Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) framework. By leveraging BNN, we are able to incorporate the predictive model's uncertainty into steganographic performance. Furthermore, we have developed an efficient training technique for BNNs by integrating an additional term to the traditional adversarial loss function. The uncertainty estimation yields numerous benefits for both steganography performance and capacity when evaluated under various metrics and predictive modeling approaches.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental properties of convection, but its effectiveness relies on accurately capturing high-frequency dynamics of turbulent fluctuations. By using advanced numerical simulations of convection, we have observed that these fluctuations extend to significantly higher frequencies than previously anticipated. Utilizing this new insight, we have found that incorporating more turbulent frequencies results in more realistic hydromagnetic simulations that closely resemble observational data. The variation in cyclic magnetic activity is more accurately explained when incorporating higher-frequency turbulent dynamics, in contrast to the assumption of limiting the analysis to lower frequencies. This finding highlights the importance of including the full range of turbulent frequencies to model dynamos effectively in stars and the Sun.

A study using the ALMA reveals molecular outflows in the center of the galaxy NGC4945, which is a highly inclined spiral galaxy with the center partially obscured. The galaxy exhibits a dense ring of molecular gas at its center, and our observations of the CS(1-0) and CS(2-1) lines provide information on the gas dynamics in the central region. By analyzing the spectrum of the CS lines, we identify two distinct components: a broad feature likely caused by outflows and a narrower, thermally broadened line. Using simulations, we determine the gas velocities and line widths associated with the outflows, which have velocities ranging from approximately 300-600 km/s. The outflowing gas forms in a region within 0.5 parsecs of the center, and its properties can be modeled as rotating in a Keplerian orbit. Assuming a total gas mass of 2.3 x 10^7 solar masses at the center, we estimate that approximately 10% of this gas resonates within the outflow region. Our simulations also model the outflow using radiative momentum and absorption maps, and our results indicate that the outflow could be driven either by the galaxy's radio jet or by shock interactions between the outflowing gas and the disk.

A magnetized plasma's quasilinear diffusion model successfully describes particle transport in various scientific and engineering fields. However, numerical solutions for the related Fokker-Planck equations present a challenge due to their non-linear nature and the wide range of spatial and temporal scales involved. A new Galerkin method has been developed, which uses a semi-iterative approach to overcome the nonlinearity in the quasilinear equation through an operator splitting technique. This method has been tested and validated by recovering known asymptotic solutions and accurately modeling the stochastic motion of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field, as well as an electron in a magnetic trap. Additionally, the method has been applied to the model for low-frequency electron turbulence in tokamaks, which displays a low-conversion rate from drift instability into turbulent transport.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods with non-uniform stepsize SGLMs, and prove that they converge at the same rate as their uniform stepsize counterparts. This is further validated through experiments involving air drag models and bifurcations, revealing improved performance when adapting to changing problem dynamics by using variable stepsize SGLMs on non-uniform grids.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and the left regularity of the semigroup T.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool for determining interaction cross sections between dimuonium (true muonium) and matter, also computing corresponding form factors. With input parameters including muon mass, dimuonium energy, and an atomic nucleus' charge form factor, MuMuPy produces tables showing interaction probabilities and form factor graphs. Developed in Python, the code is available under a free license and can be accessed via the MuMuPy website or the PyPI package.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards (relative performance) and in the context of broader market conditions (absolute performance). The typical metric for absolute performance is the risk-free rate-adjusted return. Meanwhile, the return of the benchmark portfolio minus that of the investment portfolio gauges relative performance. The power utility function, which incorporates both absolute and relative performance, provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating portfolio performance. This paper will present a model for achieving optimal portfolio allocation under a combined absolute and relative performance power utility functions. The key assumption is that absolute performance is adjusted by the risk-free rate, and relative performance follows a geometric Brownian motion. The model assumes investors adhere to a log-utility function for both absolute and relative performances. By solving a bi-variate Bellman equation, the paper derives an explicit solution for hedging and investment strategies. The model parameters demonstrate a clear distribution effect on portfolio allocation. The study shows that in optimal portfolios, 40% to 50% of assets are allocated to a risk-free bond, 20% to 50% are invested in the worst-performing asset, and 10% to 30% are invested in the average-performing asset. The remaining assets (10% to 80%) are invested in the best-performing assets. The model also shows that as the importance of relative performance increases, the investment in the worst-performing asset rises, while that in the best-performing assets falls.
